knowledge/concepts/actor-critic.md.title: Actor-Critic
knowledge/concepts/actor-critic.md.description:
Actor-Critic methods simultaneously learn a policy and a value function to combine policy gradient and value-based reinforcement learning approaches.
Key features include using temporal difference learning for low-variance feedback, employing advantage functions to reduce variance, and supporting both on-policy and off-policy learning strategies.
These methods are widely used in continuous control tasks and reinforcement learning from human feedback to achieve scalable and stable training.
They matter because they enable agents to handle complex continuous action spaces while balancing exploration and exploitation through mechanisms like entropy regularization.
knowledge/concepts/actor-critic.md.summary: Actor-Critic methods combine policy gradient and value-based learning by simultaneously updating a policy (actor) and a value function (critic). The critic uses temporal difference learning to provide low-variance feedback, enabling scalability to continuous action spaces. Key variants include on-policy methods like A3C/A2C and PPO (which uses clipped surrogate objectives), and off-policy methods like SAC (entropy-regularized) and TD3 (twin critics to reduce overestimation). On-policy approaches offer stability but lower sample efficiency, whereas off-policy methods leverage replay buffers for higher efficiency. Advanced techniques include Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) for variance reduction, intrinsic motivation via prediction error for exploration, and multi-agent extensions like CTDE (MADDPG/MAPPO) for credit assignment. Recent theoretical advances (2025) have resolved sample complexity bounds, while applications span robotics, autonomous drones, energy management, and LLM alignment (RLHF).

knowledge/concepts/agent-framework-compa.title: Agent Framework Comparison (2026)
knowledge/concepts/agent-framework-compa.description:
This node compares top LLM agent frameworks like LangGraph and Claude Agent SDK for automation engineers.
Key features include native MCP server support, explicit graph-structured control flow, and built-in permission models.
Use cases range from production code-execution agents to research-grade multi-agent debate patterns.
It matters by helping developers select the right tool based on their specific model ecosystem and orchestration needs.
knowledge/concepts/agent-framework-compa.summary: This 2026 comparison evaluates LLM agent frameworks for automation engineers, excluding generic workflow engines. Key frameworks include Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS, Anthropic-backed), LangGraph (Python/TS, LangChain-backed), Microsoft Agent Framework (Python/.NET, Microsoft-backed), CrewAI (Python, CrewAI Inc.), OpenAI Agents SDK (Python/TS, OpenAI-backed), and LlamaIndex Agents (Python/TS, LlamaIndex-backed). The decision logic recommends the Claude Agent SDK for reliable tool-use within the Claude ecosystem, LangGraph for explicit graph control and checkpointing, CrewAI for team-of-roles mental models, Microsoft Agent Framework for multi-agent debate and Azure integration, and OpenAI Agents SDK for GPT-locked stacks. Cross-framework production reliability relies on validating structured outputs, setting execution budgets, ensuring idempotent tools, implementing observability, and maintaining eval harnesses. Frameworks should be avoided for single LLM calls, deterministic tasks, or pure RPA automation.

knowledge/concepts/agent-orchestration.m.title: Agent Orchestration
knowledge/concepts/agent-orchestration.m.description:
Agent Orchestration is the process of managing and coordinating multiple AI agents to collaborate on complex tasks.
It dynamically decomposes goals, selects appropriate agents, manages resources, and handles errors during execution.
This approach enables parallel workloads and flexible workflows beyond simple linear chaining.
It matters because it allows systems to scale complexity while maintaining control over costs and outcomes.
knowledge/concepts/agent-orchestration.m.summary: Agent Orchestration manages multiple AI agents to execute complex tasks by decomposing goals, selecting agents, monitoring progress, handling errors, and assembling results. It differs from simple chaining by supporting dynamic decomposition, parallel execution, and retry logic. Key responsibilities include task decomposition, agent selection, resource management, progress tracking, error handling, result assembly, and context injection. Common patterns include Static (pre-defined DAGs), Dynamic (LLM-driven runtime decomposition), and Reactive (event-driven triggers). Popular frameworks include Claude Code Agent tool, LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, and Claude-Flow. Communication occurs via tool-based delegation, message-based requests, or shared state blackboards. Best practices for handoffs involve concise prompts (300–500 tokens) specifying agent, task, context, success criteria, and output location. Cost optimization strategies include right-sizing models (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), limiting parallelism to three agents, focusing context, early termination, and caching. Failure handling employs retry loops with escalating priority or task skipping. This specific project utilizes the Claude Code Agent tool, a blackboard pattern, MCP servers, and a hook system for reactive automation.

knowledge/concepts/agentic-llm-workflows.title: Agentic LLM Workflows
knowledge/concepts/agentic-llm-workflows.description:
Agentic LLM Workflows is a pattern that uses specialized agents and varied models to efficiently handle complex tasks.
It optimizes costs by routing simple operations to cheap models while reserving premium models for critical decisions.
The system improves quality through dedicated agents for planning, coding, testing, and maintenance roles.
Workflow orchestration sequences these agents in simple, complex, or parallel flows to manage state effectively.
This approach matters because it delivers high-quality AI solutions at a fraction of the cost of monolithic models.
knowledge/concepts/agentic-llm-workflows.summary: Agentic LLM Workflows utilize specialized agents and differentiated models to execute complex tasks efficiently. The core strategy involves matching model capability to task complexity: using Haiku for routine operations (~70% of tasks), Sonnet for planning and implementation (~25%), Opus for critical decisions (~5%), and Ollama for simple validations when available. Agents are specialized by role into Planning (requirements, architecture), Implementation (coding, scripting, testing), and Maintenance (documentation, memory curation, code review). Workflow orchestration sequences these agents in simple, complex, or parallel flows, managed by a main session coordinator that updates working memory. Context efficiency is maintained through concise handoffs (300-500 tokens), file references instead of full content, and archiving completed work. This approach delivers significant cost savings, improved quality through iterative refinement, and scalability via parallel execution. Implementation relies on markdown-defined agents with specific model assignments, automatic quality hooks (SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse), and modular skills. Best practices emphasize spawning agents only for complex tasks, reserving premium models for critical decisions, and monitoring usage to optimize costs.

knowledge/concepts/ai-infrastructure-bud.title: AI Infrastructure Budget Configurations
knowledge/concepts/ai-infrastructure-bud.description:
AI Infrastructure Budget Configurations provide a decision framework for balancing on-premise hardware and cloud services across three budget tiers.
The solution covers entry-level proof-of-concepts, mid-tier production limits, and full-scale enterprise deployments with specific ROI timelines.
Users can select optimal strategies like used GPU clusters or multi-cloud bursts to match performance needs with total cost of ownership.
This matters because it enables teams to rapidly deploy AI workloads while minimizing financial risk and maximizing return on investment.
knowledge/concepts/ai-infrastructure-bud.summary:
This framework outlines AI infrastructure configurations for 2026 across three budget tiers (€15K–50K), balancing on-premise hardware with cloud services to optimize Total Cost of Ownership (TCO).

**Tier 1 (€15K–20K):** Targets entry-level and proof-of-concept use cases. Strategies include using used RTX 3090s with cloud bursts, single RTX 4090s with aggressive cloud reliance, or distributed clusters of three RTX 4070 Ti Super cards. These setups support models up to ~13B parameters on-premise, with larger models requiring cloud training.

**Tier 2 (€30K–35K):** Serves mid-tier production and advanced research. Options include dual RTX 4090s with multi-cloud strategies, mixed AMD MI210 and RTX 4090 ecosystems for HPC/inference workloads, or four-RTX 4090 clusters for heavy on-premise inference of models up to 65B.

**Tier 3 (€45K–50K):** Enables full enterprise deployment and intensive research. Configurations feature enterprise-grade A100 40GB/80GB cards, large distributed clusters of six RTX 4090s, or hybrid setups combining A100s with RTX 4090s. A "Full Cloud" option is also available for zero CapEx scenarios.

**Decision Logic:** Choose on-premise for continuous workloads, data sovereignty, and low latency; choose cloud for burst training and latest hardware access; adopt a hybrid approach for continuous development with occasional intensive training. Future pricing should compare current Ada/Ampere parts against emerging Blackwell generation hardware.

knowledge/concepts/automation-workflow-d.title: Automation Workflow Design Framework
knowledge/concepts/automation-workflow-d.description:
It is an ordered set of eight design decisions that transform vague process descriptions into reliable, implementation-ready automation specifications.
Key features include mapping triggers and systems, selecting an appropriate execution engine, and defining idempotency and retry policies.
Use cases span webhook-triggered flows, scheduled batch jobs, and complex multi-system automations requiring high reliability.
It matters because skipping these design steps leads to mismatched assumptions, technical debt, and workflows that break under real-world volume.
knowledge/concepts/automation-workflow-d.summary:
The Automation Workflow Design Framework is an ordered set of eight critical decisions required to transform a vague business process into a reliable, implementation-ready specification for multi-system automations (webhooks, batches, queues). Skipping any decision leads to mismatched assumptions and technical debt.

1.  **Map the process**: Define triggers, systems, data flow, branching, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) needs, failure tolerance, and volume.
2.  **Pick the engine**: Select a workflow engine (e.g., Temporal, Zapier, Airflow) that fits requirements and budget, justifying the choice against volume constraints.
3.  **Design idempotency**: Implement keys, storage, TTLs, and collision handling for every retry-prone step to ensure exactly-once execution semantics.
4.  **Retry + DLQ policy**: Define exponential backoff strategies, classify errors as transient or permanent, and establish Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) procedures for exhausted events.
5.  **Observability**: Establish structured logging, metrics, tracing, and alerts to detect silent failures and health issues.
6.  **Auth + secrets**: Determine OAuth flows, secure secret storage (never in git), rotation plans, and multi-tenant isolation.
7.  **Cost envelope**: Model per-event costs and project monthly expenses at current and 10× volume to avoid surprise bills.
8.  **Implementation skeleton + test plan**: Create engine-specific code stubs and a comprehensive test plan including unit, integration, end-to-end, chaos, and load tests.

The framework produces a standardized output document containing process descriptions, system mappings, engine rationale, step specifications, and test plans. It mandates strict "push-back checkpoints" against common pitfalls like engine mismatches, lack of idempotency, missing DLQs, and secrets in git. This discipline is essential for workflows involving two or more third-party systems or retry-prone triggers, while simple one-off scripts are exempt.

knowledge/concepts/bayesian-inference.md.title: Bayesian Inference
knowledge/concepts/bayesian-inference.md.description:
Bayesian inference is a statistical method that updates probability estimates for hypotheses as new evidence is observed.
It relies on Bayes' theorem to compute posterior distributions from prior beliefs and likelihoods while handling intractable integrals.
Approximate methods like variational inference and MCMC enable practical computation for complex generative models and multi-agent systems.
This framework underpins the Free Energy Principle, facilitates multi-agent coordination, and enhances LLM reasoning through uncertainty quantification.
knowledge/concepts/bayesian-inference.md.summary: Bayesian inference is a statistical framework that updates hypothesis probabilities using Bayes' theorem, integrating prior beliefs with observed data to compute posterior distributions. It serves as the mathematical foundation for the Free Energy Principle and Active Inference, where variational free energy minimization approximates intractable posterior calculations. Key methods include Variational Inference (optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound), Markov Chain Monte Carlo (asymptotically exact sampling), and Laplace Approximation. Applications span multi-agent coordination (e.g., BEACOF, Bayesian Delegation), LLM reasoning, knowledge graph filtering, and reinforcement learning. The approach aligns with the Bayesian Brain Hypothesis, mapping perception, action, learning, and attention to specific inference mechanisms. Challenges include computational intractability for large models and prior sensitivity, often mitigated by amortized inference, neural approximators, and hierarchical priors.

knowledge/concepts/blameless-postmortem-.title: Blameless Post-Mortem Methodology
knowledge/concepts/blameless-postmortem-.description:
A blameless post-mortem is a structured retrospective that analyzes systemic failures rather than individual errors to drive durable corrective actions.
It encourages early incident declaration and full transparency by removing fear of personal blame while maintaining accountability for action items.
This methodology applies to any user-visible outage, data loss, security breach, or significant near-miss to prevent recurrence.
It matters because it transforms isolated mistakes into organizational learning, improving system reliability and reducing future downtime.
knowledge/concepts/blameless-postmortem-.summary: A blameless post-mortem is a structured retrospective focused on systemic factors rather than individual blame, aiming to drive durable corrective actions. It is required for user-visible impacts, data loss, security incidents, near-misses, or recurring issues. The document structure includes a summary, impact metrics, an append-only timeline, detection methods, multiple contributing factors (avoiding single "root cause" framing), analysis of what went well/poorly/luckily, and specific action items categorized as prevent, detect, or mitigate. Key rules mandate avoiding individual names in causal statements, using declarative past tense, distinguishing facts from hypotheses, assigning specific owners to actions, and treating human actions as symptoms of system gaps rather than errors. Common pitfalls to avoid include treating post-mortems as theater, letting action items languish, framing incidents as single-cause, and lacking a near-miss culture.

knowledge/concepts/brand-identity-system.title: Brand Identity System Layers
knowledge/concepts/brand-identity-system.description:
Brand Identity System Layers is a top-down structural framework that prevents brand drift by connecting positioning to visual execution.
It features a positioning brief that defines audience and personality, a multi-variant logomark system with scalable clearspace rules, and a three-tier color architecture spanning digital and print spaces.
This system serves as a backbone for creating new brands or auditing existing ones to ensure consistency across all touchpoints.
It matters because it replaces subjective taste with defensible rules, ensuring the identity remains coherent within 90 days of launch.
knowledge/concepts/brand-identity-system.summary:
A modern brand identity is a constrained, seven-layer system where each layer informs the next (Positioning → Mark → Color/Type → Grid → Media → Voice/Motion). Skipping layers leads to inconsistency within 90 days.

1.  **Positioning Brief:** Defines audience, promise, personality (with anti-pairs), and competitive whitespace; serves as the constitution for all decisions.
2.  **Logomark System:** A system of marks including primary/stacked lockups, monograms, wordmarks, and submarks, defined by clearspace (relative units) and minimum sizes.
3.  **Color System:** Uses a three-tier token architecture (Primitive, Semantic, Component) and specifies colors across sRGB, P3, Adobe RGB, CMYK, Pantone, and L*a*b* to ensure cross-medium accuracy.
4.  **Typography:** Selects one display and one text family (or superfamily), defines modular scales, licenses, pairing tests, and system font fallbacks.
5.  **Layout & Grid:** Establishes baseline grids (4px/8px), column grids (12-col web/6-col print), and unified spacing scales.
6.  **Media:** Provides one-page direction documents for photography, illustration, and iconography, including AI prompt anatomy.
7.  **Voice & Motion:** Documents tone variations by context and defines signature motion transitions (e.g., app-open, error shake).

**Validation & Handoff:** Systems must pass a checklist covering app icons, social avatars, print, web, light/dark variants, and accessibility (WCAG). Audits score legibility, contrast, license coverage, and file hygiene. Production handoffs deliver DTCG token files, organized folder structures, consistent naming, and license tracking. Common failures include treating logos as isolated assets, ignoring cross-space color values, and neglecting recurring type licensing costs.

knowledge/concepts/build-vs-buy-decision.title: Build vs Buy Decision Framework for Indies
knowledge/concepts/build-vs-buy-decision.description:
This framework helps indie founders overcome the bias to build everything in-house by scoring six axes to reveal hidden maintenance and opportunity costs.
It uses a 1–5 scoring system across dimensions like core product distance, time to ship, maintenance burden, lock-in risk, and vendor cost to generate a defensible decision.
The tool is designed for solo founders and small teams evaluating whether to develop custom features or purchase existing SaaS solutions for their products.
It matters because it prevents founders from wasting years on non-core code that drains attention and prevents them from missing better opportunities to ship value.
knowledge/concepts/build-vs-buy-decision.summary:
**Build vs Buy Decision Framework for Indies**

**Core Principle:** Indie founders default to "build," which is incorrect ~70% of the time. Building incurs hidden ongoing costs (maintenance, security, edge cases) where the first 80% of work takes a week and the remaining 20% takes two years. This framework exposes these costs to force defensible decisions.

**Scoring System (6 Axes, 1–5 each):**
Sum the scores (Range 6–30) to determine the recommendation.
1.  **Distance From Core Product:** Score 5 (IS core) = Build; Score 1 (Infrastructure) = Buy. Generic capabilities (auth, billing) should be bought to free time for differentiating features.
2.  **Time To Ship:** Score 5 (>1 month) = High cost; Score 1 (<1 day) = Trivial. Account for realistic estimates (founders underestimate by 2–3×) and opportunity cost.
3.  **Ongoing Maintenance:** Score 5 (Security/On-call) = High cost; Score 1 (Write once) = Low cost. Calculate hours/year × hourly rate as part of build cost.
4.  **Vendor Lock-In Risk:** Score 5 (No export/proprietary) = High risk; Score 1 (Interchangeable) = Low risk. Mitigate by choosing open formats.
5.  **Vendor Cost Trajectory:** Score 5 (Usage-priced) = High risk; Score 1 (Free/One-time) = No risk. Note that revenue-based pricing (e.g., Stripe) often makes building cheaper only at massive scale.
6.  **Capability Risk:** Score 5 (Catastrophic failure) = High risk; Score 1 (None) = Low risk. High risk (payments, auth) usually mandates buying due to asymmetry of failure costs.

**Recommendation Thresholds:**
*   **6–12:** Buy/Integrate.
*   **13–18:** Buy unless there are ≥3 strong signals to build.
*   **19–24:** Genuine trade-off; apply tiebreakers.
*   **25–30:** Build (Core product or trivial).

**Tiebreakers (For Scores 13–24):**
*   **MRR Stage:** <$5K (Buy almost all); $5–25K (Buy default); $25K+ (Afford to build).
*   **Runway:** If <6 months, never build.
*   **Team Capacity:** If context-switching across 4+ areas, buy.
*   **Reversibility:** If switching from buy→build costs <2 weeks, start by buying.

**Category Defaults:**
*   **Buy:** Payments, Auth, Email, Analytics, Error Tracking, Support Chat, CMS, Status Page.
*   **Build:** Marketing Site, Onboarding Flow, Core Product Features.
*   **Hybrid:** Search (use managed services).

**Anti-Patterns to Avoid:**
*   Ignoring real maintenance costs (time × rate).
*   Building for "full control" or because it is "fun."
*   Underestimating the irreversibility of deep integrations (auth, billing).
*   Treating self-hosted open source as "free" (it is "buy" with high implementation cost).

**Review Trigger:** Re-evaluate decisions when specific changes occur (price doubling, hitting $25K MRR, deprecation notices, integration breaks).

knowledge/concepts/chunking-strategies-l.title: Chunking Strategies for LLM and RAG Systems
knowledge/concepts/chunking-strategies-l.description:
Chunking strategies split documents into smaller pieces to optimize retrieval quality in LLM and RAG systems.
Recursive character splitting preserves document structure by splitting at natural boundaries like paragraphs or sentences.
Semantic chunking analyzes meaning shifts between sentences to create topic-aligned chunks with higher recall.
These strategies matter because poor chunking can cause up to a 9% drop in retrieval performance.
They are essential for balancing context preservation, embedding limits, and retrieval accuracy in AI applications.
knowledge/concepts/chunking-strategies-l.summary:
Chunking splits documents into smaller pieces for embedding and indexing, directly impacting retrieval quality; poor strategies can reduce recall by up to 9%. The core tradeoff involves balancing context preservation against chunk size: too small loses context and increases noise, while too large reduces precision and slows retrieval.

**Key Strategies:**
1. **Recursive Character Splitting**: Splits at natural boundaries (paragraphs, sentences) using a hierarchy of separators. It preserves document structure and is the reliable default for articles and technical docs, achieving 88-89% recall.
2. **Semantic Chunking**: Uses embeddings to detect topic shifts based on similarity drops. It offers the highest quality for dense documents (2-3% better recall than recursive splitting) but is computationally expensive and requires threshold tuning.
3. **Page-Level Chunking**: Treats each page as a chunk, ideal for PDFs, financial reports, and legal documents where pagination aligns with logical units. It yields the highest accuracy (0.648) with low variance for paginated content.
4. **Sentence-Based Chunking**: Groups sentences to meet size targets, maintaining natural flow. Best suited for conversational data and Q&A datasets.
5. **Size-Based (Fixed) Chunking**: Splits by fixed character or token counts. It is the fastest and simplest for prototyping but fragments context and ignores document structure.
6. **LLM-Based Chunking**: Uses an LLM to identify logical break points. Highly context-aware for unusual documents but costly and slow, suitable only for high-value or experimental use.
7. **Late Chunking**: Embeds the full document first before extracting chunks, preserving cross-chunk references and pronoun accuracy. An emerging technique for documents with long-range dependencies.

**Decision Framework**: Select **Page-Level** for paginated PDFs; **Semantic** for dense unstructured text; **Sentence-Based** for conversational data; **Recursive** or **Size-Based** for simple homogeneous content.

knowledge/concepts/churn-taxonomy-and-ta.title: Churn Taxonomy and Reduction Tactics
knowledge/concepts/churn-taxonomy-and-ta.description: Churn Taxonomy and Reduction Tactics is a framework for solo SaaS founders to decompose customer loss into voluntary and involuntary categories. It features mechanical fixes like smart card retries for involuntary churn and strategic survey-based analysis for voluntary cancellations. This approach matters because treating all churn as one bucket wastes resources, whereas targeted tactics can double steady-state MRR by reducing monthly churn from 5% to 2%. The use case involves implementing specific retention flows such as pause options, downgrade paths, and post-cancel email sequences to recover revenue and understand root causes.
knowledge/concepts/churn-taxonomy-and-ta.summary: Churn is a critical metric for SaaS founders where reducing monthly churn from 5% to 2% doubles steady-state MRR at the same acquisition rate. The first step is decomposition into a 2x2 matrix: Voluntary (Account-level cancellations, Usage-level silent churn) vs. Involuntary (Payment failures). Involuntary churn (20–40% of total) is mechanical leakage fixed by Smart Retries, pre-dunning emails, in-app banners, and account-updater services. Voluntary account-level churn requires analyzing cancellation reasons (bad fit, missing feature, bug, price, competitor) via surveys, offering pauses or downgrades instead of discounts, and avoiding immediate retention offers. Voluntary usage-level churn is detected by lack of engagement events and managed via re-engagement emails and proactive pause offers. The Quick-Ratio ((new + expansion MRR) / (churned + contraction MRR)) serves as the primary health indicator, with ratios >4 indicating growth and <1 requiring immediate churn focus. Finally, specific churn clusters (e.g., month 2–3, annual renewal, usage limits) often signal underlying pricing or onboarding issues, while win-back efforts should be limited to two attempts within 30–90 days post-cancel.

knowledge/concepts/claude-code-workflows.title: Claude Code Workflows Feature — Premade Workflow Integration
knowledge/concepts/claude-code-workflows.description:
This feature introduces deterministic JavaScript orchestration scripts in Claude Code v2.1.154+ that spawn subagents using primitives like `agent()`, `parallel()`, and `pipeline()`.
It supports triggers including the `ultracode` keyword, natural language requests, and saved workflow files for both user and project scopes.
Use cases include bundled deep research tasks that cross-check web sources and custom multi-agent pipelines for complex, parameterized automation.
It matters because it enforces strict determinism by blocking random functions and filesystem access while allowing concurrent execution up to 16 agents per run.
knowledge/concepts/claude-code-workflows.summary: Claude Code v2.1.154+ introduces a built-in `Workflow` tool for deterministic JavaScript orchestration, available on all paid plans and major APIs. Workflows are triggered by the `ultracode` keyword, `/effort ultracode`, natural language requests, or saved workflow invocations (`/<name>`). Bundled workflows like `/deep-research` are included, while project-scoped saved workflows reside in `.claude/workflows/` and must declare metadata starting with `export const meta`. The API provides primitives for spawning subagents (`agent`), parallel execution (`parallel`), pipelines (`pipeline`), and phases (`phase`, `log`), with a token budget tracker and global `args` parameterization. Key constraints include a limit of 16 concurrent agents, no mid-run user input, blocked randomization functions, and subagents inheriting session tool allowlists. Discovery relies on structural routing via `meta` descriptions, skill wrappers invoking `Workflow({name})`, and a shipped keyword-suggest hook that dynamically matches `keywords` arrays in workflow metadata without auto-launching. Several candidate premade workflows (e.g., audit, bug-hunt, onboard) and project-specific launcher tabs remain design candidates and are not yet shipped.

knowledge/concepts/common-stats-pitfalls.title: Common Statistical Pitfalls
knowledge/concepts/common-stats-pitfalls.description:
This node catalogs frequent statistical errors in published science to serve as a pre-submission checklist for quantitative papers.
It addresses multiple uncorrected comparisons by recommending FWER or FDR control methods like Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg.
The content warns against the garden of forking paths by advocating for preregistration and multiverse analysis to separate exploratory from confirmatory work.
It defines p-hacking as the practice of continuing data collection until significance is reached and suggests reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals instead.
Use this guide to validate research integrity and prevent false positives before manuscript submission.
It matters because these common mistakes, rather than exotic methods, are the primary drivers of failed statistical inference in modern science.
knowledge/concepts/common-stats-pitfalls.summary: This node catalogs high-frequency statistical errors in published science, serving as a pre-submission checklist. The "Big Six" include: (1) Multiple comparisons without correction (fix: FWER/FDR control); (2) Garden of Forking Paths where analytical choices inflate error (fix: preregistration, specification curves); (3) P-hacking via data dredging (fix: pre-defined stopping rules, effect sizes); (4) Simpson's Paradox/confounding (fix: causal DAGs, stratification); (5) Pseudoreplication treating non-independent units as independent (fix: mixed-effects models); and (6) confusing significance with practical importance (fix: reporting effect sizes with CIs). Additional critical pitfalls include regression to the mean, survivorship bias, optional stopping, HARKing, stepwise variable selection, and over-reliance on standardized effects. The core corrections involve preregistration, identifying the experimental unit, using appropriate multiple testing corrections, and prioritizing effect sizes over p-values.

knowledge/concepts/constitutional-ai.md.title: Constitutional AI
knowledge/concepts/constitutional-ai.md.description:
Constitutional AI is Anthropic's self-supervised alignment method that uses AI feedback guided by written principles instead of human labeling.
It replaces expensive and risky human red-teaming with a two-phase process of self-critique and AI preference labeling.
The approach fine-tunes models using a constitution of ethical principles derived from sources like the UN Declaration of Human Rights.
This technique reduces the need for human raters while improving transparency and scalability in training harmless AI assistants.
knowledge/concepts/constitutional-ai.md.summary: Constitutional AI (CAI) is Anthropic's self-supervised alignment method that replaces extensive human labeling with AI feedback guided by a written set of principles ("a constitution"). Published by Bai et al. (2022), it forms the foundation of Claude models by substituting the human preference step in standard RLHF with model-generated feedback. The process involves two phases: Phase 1 (SL-CAI) uses a self-critique loop where the model iteratively critiques and revises harmful responses based on constitutional principles before fine-tuning; Phase 2 (RLAIF) generates AI-labeled preference pairs to train a reward model, which is then used for RL fine-tuning. The constitution, drawn from sources like the UN Declaration of Human Rights, explicitly defines "harmlessness," enabling scalable supervision with reduced human cost. Key results include models that are virtually never evasive, show stronger resistance to red-teaming, and better align helpfulness with harmlessness. While production systems often combine human labels for factuality with RLAIF for harmlessness, limitations include the quality of the feedback model, potential bias reinforcement, and cultural nuances. DPO can replace the PPO stage in RLAIF, though combining CAI self-improvement with DPO risks model collapse.

knowledge/concepts/default-on-unparseabl.title: Default-on-unparseable + early-return makes locale fallbacks unreachable
knowledge/concepts/default-on-unparseabl.description:
This node describes a bug where parsing defaults and early returns prevent locale-specific fallbacks from executing on non-English Windows systems.
Key features include treating unparseable output as a distinct value rather than a default, deferring default logic to the end of a fallback chain, and verifying claims about localized system outputs.
The use case involves correctly identifying disabled scheduled tasks on international Windows versions where standard parsing markers are localized.
It matters because failing to route to fallbacks causes misreporting of system states, such as falsely reporting a disabled task as enabled.
knowledge/concepts/default-on-unparseabl.summary: In `vct-hub/src/boot.rs`, parsing `schtasks` output defaulted to `Enabled` when English markers were missing, then immediately early-returned on that value, bypassing the locale-invariant PowerShell fallback. This caused disabled tasks on non-English Windows (where `schtasks` localizes output) to be incorrectly reported as enabled. The fix requires returning a distinct `None`/`Option` for unparseable cases rather than coercing them to a default, ensuring the fallback chain is consulted. Defaults should only be applied as the final step after all reliable sources fail, and tests must verify unparseable cases against the fallback route using realistic localized fixtures.

knowledge/concepts/diagnosing-non-determ.title: Diagnosing Non-Deterministic Results
knowledge/concepts/diagnosing-non-determ.description:
This node provides a diagnostic ladder to identify and fix the seven common sources of reproducibility drift in computational science.
It guides users to first characterize drift magnitude via output diffs before tracing the cause to specific sources like unseeded RNGs or parallel workers.
The primary use case is resolving complaints about non-reproducible results by distinguishing between stochastic behavior, numerical instability, and genuine bugs.
It matters because it transforms vague reproducibility failures into actionable fixes by matching observed drift patterns to their distinct fingerprints.
knowledge/concepts/diagnosing-non-determ.summary: Diagnosing non-deterministic results requires characterizing drift magnitude first to classify the source, then applying specific fixes. Drift types include: bit-equivalent (user error), floating-point reduction order ($\sim 10^{-12}$), single-precision/optimiser issues ($\sim 10^{-5}$), cluster label permutation (not a bug), unseeded RNGs ($>1\%$), input-dependent numerical instability, and cross-machine library/hardware differences. Fixes involve seeding all RNGs (numpy, random, torch, sklearn), configuring parallel worker seeds, pinning thread counts, enabling GPU deterministic algorithms (accepting performance hits), using partition-invariant metrics for clustering, adding numerical regularisation, and using pinned containers for cross-machine consistency.

knowledge/concepts/dimensional-analysis-.title: Dimensional Analysis and Equation Verification
knowledge/concepts/dimensional-analysis-.description:
It is a systematic set of four independent sanity checks used to verify physical derivations and numerical results before submission.
Key features include ensuring dimensional homogeneity, testing limiting behaviors, checking conservation laws, and validating order-of-magnitude estimates.
Use cases span from verifying the Schrödinger equation to collapsing complex engineering problems into dimensionless groups like the Reynolds number.
It matters because these cheap checks catch distinct classes of errors like sign mistakes or missing prefactors that single tests might miss.
knowledge/concepts/dimensional-analysis-.summary:
Before trusting a derivation, four independent sanity checks must pass: dimensional homogeneity, limiting/boundary behaviour, conservation/symmetry, and order-of-magnitude verification. These checks catch distinct error classes (e.g., sign errors, missing prefactors, unit mismatches) and form a necessary acceptance test.

1. **Dimensional Homogeneity**: All terms in an equation must share identical base dimensions (SI: M, L, T, Θ, I, N, J). Functions like exp, log, and trig require dimensionless arguments. The Buckingham π theorem reduces $n$ variables with $k$ dimensions to $n-k$ dimensionless groups (e.g., Reynolds, Péclet numbers).
2. **Limiting/Boundary Behaviour**: Equations must recover known physics in characteristic limits (e.g., $v \to 0$ recovers Newtonian mechanics from relativity; $\hbar \to 0$ recovers classical mechanics).
3. **Conservation Laws and Symmetries**: Expressions must respect conservation of energy, momentum, charge, probability, and mass, as well as system symmetries (parity, rotation).
4. **Order-of-Magnitude with Canonical Numbers**: Substituting representative values should yield expected magnitudes. Common offsets indicate specific errors: $10^{23}$ (mole vs molecule), $2\pi$ (angular frequency vs Hz), $4\pi$ (SI vs Gaussian units), and missing constants like $k_B$ or $\hbar$.

knowledge/concepts/dpo-direct-preference.title: DPO - Direct Preference Optimization
knowledge/concepts/dpo-direct-preference.description:
Direct Preference Optimization is a supervised-learning-style alignment method that removes the need for a separate reward model and reinforcement learning loop.
It achieves approximately 40% faster training and 60% lower compute costs compared to traditional PPO-based RLHF by using a closed-form mapping.
The technique is widely adopted by major models like Llama 3 and Zephyr for tasks such as summarization and single-turn dialogue.
While it offers high stability and simplicity, it is limited by its offline nature and dependency on the reference policy.
knowledge/concepts/dpo-direct-preference.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a preference-based alignment method introduced by Rafailov et al. (NeurIPS 2023) that eliminates the need for a separate reward model and reinforcement learning loop by deriving a closed-form mapping from the RLHF objective. This enables supervised-learning-style training that is approximately 40% faster and 60% cheaper than PPO-based RLHF. DPO reparameterizes the reward function using the log-probability ratio between the policy and a reference model, implicitly encoding reward without explicit scalar values. While DPO offers high stability, computational efficiency, and simplicity, it is limited by its offline nature (inability to discover failure modes not in the training data) and dependency on the reference policy. Widely adopted in major models like Llama 3 Instruct and Zephyr, DPO has spawned numerous variants (e.g., IPO, KTO, ORPO) to address specific issues like reference model removal or noisy annotations, though debates continue regarding its suitability for high-stakes domains compared to PPO.

knowledge/concepts/end-of-cycle-dedup-sw.title: End-of-cycle dedup sweep — what to extract pre-tag vs defer to next cycle
knowledge/concepts/end-of-cycle-dedup-sw.description:
This end-of-cycle dedup sweep identifies and resolves code duplication that predates release cycles or accumulates across tracks.
It extracts byte-identical or write-equivalent functions when consolidated implementations exist and tests are ready.
The process defers extraction for release-critical orchestration routines or changes requiring new behavioral tests.
Using a single grep to histogram function names enables cheap discovery of genuine copies versus acceptable delegates.
This discipline reduces regression risk by consolidating copy-paste consistency before tagging while managing backlog for complex stateful code.
knowledge/concepts/end-of-cycle-dedup-sw.summary: In multi-track release cycles, per-track "extract before duplicate" rules miss duplications that predate the cycle or span across tracks. A dedicated end-of-cycle sweep (Track J) addresses these by using a function-name histogram to identify candidates, which are then triaged as delegates, domain coincidences, script constraints, or genuine copies requiring extraction. Extraction pre-tag is mandated only when bodies are byte-identical/equivalent, a consolidated implementation exists (or is <100 lines), existing names can serve as delegates, and tests cover all surfaces. Extraction is deferred for release-critical orchestration with heavy mutable state, behavior-changing changes requiring new tests, or cases where value is deferred to the next cycle to mitigate regression risk. The v0.2.54 release extracted helper families meeting all criteria while deferring large `main()` and self-heal routines. Crucially, the sweep must re-run the histogram against the merged tree to catch cross-track residues, as per-track verifiers may miss duplicates in adjacent crates not within their scan scope.

knowledge/concepts/experimental-design-f.title: Experimental Design Framework
knowledge/concepts/experimental-design-f.description:
The Experimental Design Framework is a pre-data collection checklist ensuring defensible studies by answering nine critical questions.
It mandates refining vague ideas into falsifiable quantitative claims that include specific subject, intervention, and outcome details.
The framework requires explicitly identifying the independent experimental unit to prevent statistical pseudoreplication errors.
It enforces the inclusion of domain-specific controls matched to treatment groups to ensure result interpretability.
This structured approach prevents wasted lab effort and retractions caused by irreproducible findings.
knowledge/concepts/experimental-design-f.summary: A defensible experimental design requires answering nine questions before data collection to prevent irreproducibility and waste. The pipeline mandates: (1) refining the hypothesis into a falsifiable quantitative claim including subject, intervention, comparator, outcome, SESOI, and timing; (2) explicitly identifying the independent experimental unit to avoid pseudoreplication; (3) enumerating domain-specific controls matched 1:1 to treatments; (4) computing sample size via explicit power analysis based on SESOI, variability, and ethical minimums; (5) specifying randomisation methods, tools, block sizes, stratification, and allocation concealment; (6) defining blinding levels (subject, experimenter, outcome assessor, or analyst) to mitigate bias; (7) listing and handling confounders (biological, operator, environmental) via elimination, stratification, adjustment, or sensitivity analysis, guided by a causal DAG; (8) preregistering the primary analysis plan including hypotheses, design, sampling, variables, and inference criteria; and (9) locking the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) covering tests, assumptions, corrections, and missing data handling. Final feasibility checks include sample availability, pilot variance estimation, ethical compliance (3Rs, IRB, biosafety), and inclusion of sex as a biological variable. Reporting must adhere to field-specific standards such as ARRIVE 2.0, CONSORT, STROBE, and PRISMA.

knowledge/concepts/fine-tuning-technique.title: Fine-Tuning Techniques for Open-Source LLMs
knowledge/concepts/fine-tuning-technique.description:
Fine-tuning techniques adapt pre-trained large language models to specific tasks without requiring full retraining.
Parameter-efficient methods like LoRA and QLoRA drastically reduce VRAM needs, enabling training on consumer hardware.
These approaches allow organizations to customize models for domain-specific tasks using affordable equipment like an RTX 4090.
They matter because they democratize AI development by making high-quality model customization accessible and cost-effective.
knowledge/concepts/fine-tuning-technique.summary: Fine-tuning adapts pre-trained LLMs to specific tasks efficiently without full retraining, enabling customization on consumer hardware. **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) reduces trainable parameters by learning delta matrices (rank 8-64), offering minimal memory overhead and composability but with slightly lower quality than full tuning. **QLoRA** combines LoRA with 4-bit quantization, allowing fine-tuning of 70B models on a single RTX 4090 (48GB VRAM) compared to 400GB for full training, trading slight quality loss for massive memory savings. Other methods include Prefix Tuning, Adapter Layers, and Prompt Tuning, though LoRA and QLoRA are the production standards. Recommendations for 2025 prioritize QLoRA for single-GPU setups (<48GB) and full tuning for budget-unconstrained scenarios requiring maximum quality. Tools like Axolotl and LLaMA-Factory support these workflows, while platforms like SiliconFlow offer cloud-based alternatives. Benchmarking shows QLoRA achieves 95-98% quality parity with full tuning, making it the default choice for democratizing LLM customization.

knowledge/concepts/flashattention.md.title: FlashAttention
knowledge/concepts/flashattention.md.description:
FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that reduces memory footprint and improves speed by processing data in tiles within fast on-chip SRAM.
It achieves mathematically identical results to standard attention while avoiding the need to materialize large N×N matrices in high-bandwidth memory.
The technique trades compute for memory through tiling, online softmax, and backward recomputation to overcome GPU memory bandwidth bottlenecks.
This approach enables significantly faster training, lower memory usage, and the ability to process much longer sequences in transformer models.
knowledge/concepts/flashattention.md.summary:
FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm introduced by Dao et al. (NeurIPS 2022) that replaces the memory-bandwidth-bound standard attention with an SRAM-efficient tiling approach. By processing Q, K, V in blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM and using online softmax with backward recomputation, it reduces memory complexity from O(N²) to O(N) and HBM traffic from O(N²) to O(N²d/M). This yields 2-4x training speedups, 5-10x memory reductions, and enables 10x longer sequences.

The technology evolved through four versions:
*   **v1**: Established the core tiling and recomputation strategy.
*   **v2**: Improved work partitioning, reduced non-matmul FLOPs, and enabled multi-head parallelism.
*   **v3**: Optimized for Hopper (H100) using warp-specialized async execution, interleaved matmul/softmax, and FP8 incoherent processing, achieving 75-85% of theoretical peak FLOPs.
*   **v4**: Targets Blackwell GPUs with redesigned async pipelines, software-emulated exponentials, and BF16-first support.

FlashInfer extends this paradigm for production serving, supporting block-sparse KV caches and JIT compilation to reduce latency by up to 69%. While FlashAttention is universally adopted in major LLMs (GPT-4, Llama, Mistral) and inference frameworks (vLLM, TGI), it requires architecture-specific kernel reimplementations and incurs slight FLOP overhead due to recomputation.

knowledge/concepts/function-calling-reli.title: Function Calling Reliability Patterns
knowledge/concepts/function-calling-reli.description:
Function Calling Reliability Patterns are production-grade strategies designed to stabilize LLM tool use against common failures like malformed JSON or wrong tool selection.
Key features include enforcing strict JSON schemas with `additionalProperties: false`, implementing server-side validation where possible, and running client-side validation loops with error feedback.
These patterns are used in enterprise applications to ensure that AI agents execute complex workflows without crashing due to hallucinated structures or semantic mistakes.
They matter because they transform brittle demo behavior into robust production systems capable of handling real-world data constraints and user expectations.
knowledge/concepts/function-calling-reli.summary: Function calling reliability requires addressing four failure modes: malformed JSON, schema violations, wrong tool selection, and infinite loops/no-calls. Key patterns include: (1) Strict JSON schemas with `additionalProperties: false` and concrete types, leveraging server-side enforcement where available; (2) Validation-correct loops that feed errors back to the model to resolve >90% of failures in one round; (3) Tool description discipline using explicit triggers, disambiguation, side effects, and preconditions; (4) Pre-call guards to enforce business invariants and authorization; (5) Tool-call budgets (tokens, calls, time) to prevent loops; (6) Error-as-data, returning structured errors instead of exceptions to allow model adaptation; (7) Eval harnesses with ~30+ scenarios for regression testing; and (8) Observability hooks for metrics and tracing. Anti-patterns to avoid include relying on models for retries, using `Any` types, returning giant blobs, creating mega-tools, and trusting outputs without validation.

knowledge/concepts/gdpr-eu-vat-lite-for-.title: GDPR and EU VAT Lite for Solo Founders
knowledge/concepts/gdpr-eu-vat-lite-for-.description:
This operational checklist provides a lightweight compliance framework for solo founders running self-serve SaaS with under $50K MRR and EU customers.
It replaces generic legal advice with a tractable weekend project focused on creating a defensible posture against regulatory complaints and audit questions.
Key features include a customized privacy policy listing actual sub-processors, a cookie consent strategy favoring server-side analytics, and a ready-to-send Data Processing Agreement for B2B deals.
The use case is specifically for indie developers needing to secure EU customers without incurring disproportionate legal costs or missing mandatory VAT obligations.
It matters because ignoring these basics risks severe fines, lost B2B contracts, and reputational damage from a single disgruntled customer complaint.
knowledge/concepts/gdpr-eu-vat-lite-for-.summary:
This guide provides an operational checklist for solo founders running self-serve SaaS with under $50K MRR and EU customers, emphasizing that while fines are severe, regulators rarely pursue small indies absent a complaint. The core strategy prioritizes immediate readiness for B2B deals and manageable VAT compliance.

**GDPR Compliance (Defensible-Indie Edition):**
1.  **Privacy Policy:** Must explicitly list actual data processors (e.g., Stripe, email providers, analytics tools), define legal bases, specify retention periods, and provide a single contact email for user rights.
2.  **Cookie Consent:** Required only for non-essential tracking (e.g., Google Analytics); strictly necessary session/payment cookies do not need a banner. Server-side analytics and first-party cookies are preferred to avoid consent requirements.
3.  **Data Processing Agreement (DPA):** A one-page DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) must be ready within 24 hours of a B2B customer's request; lacking one kills the deal.
4.  **Right to Erasure:** Implement a self-serve delete button that removes data from primary databases immediately and purges backups within a reasonable cycle (e.g., 30 days). Anonymize analytics events rather than attempting deletion.
5.  **Breach Notification:** Establish a process to detect breaches and notify the relevant Data Protection Authority (DPA) within 72 hours.

**EU VAT Strategy:**
*   **B2C Sales:** VAT is owed in the customer's country. For founders under $50K MRR, using a **Merchant of Record (MoR)** like Lemon Squeezy or Paddle is the recommended path to avoid the administrative burden of the One-Stop Shop (OSS).
*   **B2B Sales:** Apply the **Reverse Charge** mechanism by validating the customer's VAT number via VIES and including it on the invoice; no VAT is collected by the seller.

**Priorities:**
1.  Create a DPA and Privacy Policy to gate B2B deals.
2.  Adopt an MoR if EU revenue exceeds 10%.
3.  Switch to privacy-preserving analytics.
4.  Ensure functional account deletion flows.
5.  Maintain breach notification templates and cookie banners only if necessary.

**US Context:** Most indie SaaS is out of scope for CCPA/CPRA unless specific thresholds are met, but adding a "Do Not Sell" link is cost-free. HIPAA requires a BAA and should be avoided until legal counsel is affordable.

knowledge/concepts/generic-per-module-db.title: Generic Per-Module DB Architecture
knowledge/concepts/generic-per-module-db.description:
This architecture replaces non-scalable per-column database patterns with a generic table keyed by project and module IDs.
It eliminates the need for new SQL migrations and schema changes whenever a new paid or free module is added.
The design ensures that adding modules remains a pure manifest and container concern rather than a launcher database concern.
This pattern applies to multiple tables including module_installs and module_ports to support the v0.2.26 dispatcher.
knowledge/concepts/generic-per-module-db.summary: The Generic Per-Module DB Architecture replaces the non-scalable `projects.rl_port` column with the `module_ports` table (introduced in Migration 017, v0.2.26) to support an open-ended pipeline of paid modules without schema changes. This design establishes a complete generic state surface consisting of four tables keyed by `(project_id, module_id)`: `module_installs` (install state), `module_settings` (user config), `module_weights_state` (bundle metadata), and `module_ports` (HTTP port allocation). The architecture enforces a single-writer principle, where each table is written exclusively by a specific engine (e.g., installer, GUI, hub poller, supervisor) to ensure race-free allocation and predictable debugging. Crucially, `module_ports` tracks allocation rather than license state, allowing the system to decouple container startup from license validation. This enables a "zero-launcher-code" workflow for new paid modules, where adding a module requires only manifest updates and container deployment, as the launcher reads from the generic tables and executes actions via the declarative-action dispatcher.

knowledge/concepts/graphrag-pattern.md.title: GraphRAG Pattern
knowledge/concepts/graphrag-pattern.md.description:
GraphRAG is a Microsoft Research approach that augments standard retrieval with graph-structured knowledge to answer complex global questions.
It builds an LLM-generated knowledge graph over a corpus to enable community-level summarization and multi-hop reasoning.
The system uses hierarchical community detection and parallel report generation to synthesize answers across entire document collections.
This pattern matters because it overcomes standard RAG's inability to handle questions requiring synthesis across many disparate sources.
knowledge/concepts/graphrag-pattern.md.summary: GraphRAG (Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a Microsoft Research approach that enhances standard RAG by integrating graph-structured knowledge to answer complex, global questions spanning entire document corporuses. It operates through an indexing phase involving entity/relationship extraction, community detection via the Leiden algorithm, multi-level community summarization, and hierarchical report generation. During the query phase, it performs local searches by retrieving entity neighborhoods combined with vector chunks, and global searches by synthesizing parallel community summaries. Compared to standard RAG, GraphRAG excels at global questions and explainability but incurs higher build costs and latency. It integrates with Weaviate for hybrid retrieval and includes variants like Local GraphRAG, DRIFT Search, HopRAG, Agentic RAG, and LightRAG. Key limitations include high indexing costs, dependency on extraction model quality, and unsuitability for small document sets.

knowledge/concepts/hook-discipline-vct-d.title: Hook Discipline — VCT_DISABLE_HOOKS Escape Hatch
knowledge/concepts/hook-discipline-vct-d.description:
This is an environment variable-driven kill-switch that allows all shell hooks in the vibecoded-orchestrator to exit cleanly without executing their logic.
It enforces a strict guard pattern in every hook file and uses CI tests to prevent new hooks from bypassing this safety mechanism.
The feature enables rapid debugging of misbehaving hooks, prevents CI noise from background services, and ensures clean installations when hooks are disabled.
It matters because it provides a single-knob solution to disable hooks without editing code, maintaining trust and reliability across different execution environments.
knowledge/concepts/hook-discipline-vct-d.summary: The `VCT_DISABLE_HOOKS` escape hatch is an environment-variable-driven kill-switch that allows all shell hooks in `.claude/hooks/*.sh` to exit cleanly (status 0) without executing their logic. This guard is placed immediately after the credential-scrub block to ensure secrets are never leaked, even if a hook fails between scrubbing and the guard check. Enforced by CI tests (`tests/test_hooks_disable_guard.py`), the discipline mandates that every top-level hook includes this guard, while helper libraries are excluded. Additionally, hooks using `set -e` must also enable `pipefail`. This mechanism facilitates debugging, prevents CI noise from external service probes, and ensures a clean installation path by allowing users to defer hook execution until a live session.

knowledge/concepts/hpc-job-submission-pa.title: HPC Job Submission Patterns
knowledge/concepts/hpc-job-submission-pa.description:
HPC Job Submission Patterns define standard practices for submitting computational tasks across major schedulers like SLURM, PBS, SGE, and LSF.
Key features include a scheduler cheat sheet for command syntax, resource estimation heuristics for CPU, memory, and GPU allocation, and a reusable SLURM template for job scripts.
This knowledge applies to researchers and engineers running parallel workloads on academic and national-lab clusters to ensure efficient resource utilization.
It matters because accurate resource estimation prevents job failures due to over-allocation, while standardized patterns streamline reproducible and scalable scientific computing.
knowledge/concepts/hpc-job-submission-pa.summary:
**Overview**: Academic and national-lab clusters in 2026 primarily use **SLURM**, with legacy systems including PBS/Torque/OpenPBS, SGE/UGE/Grid Engine, and IBM's LSF.

**Scheduler Cheat Sheet**:
*   **SLURM**: Submit via `sbatch`, header `#SBATCH`, status `squeue`, cancel `scancel`.
*   **PBS/Torque/OpenPBS**: Submit via `qsub`, header `#PBS`, status `qstat`, cancel `qdel`.
*   **SGE/UGE/Grid Engine**: Submit via `qsub`, header `#$`, status `qstat`, cancel `qdel`.
*   **LSF**: Submit via `bsub`, header `#BSUB`, status `bjobs`, cancel `bkill`.
*   **Detection**: Use `which sbatch qsub bsub` or `module avail`. Site specifics (partitions, accounts) are found in `/etc/motd` or documentation.

**Resource Estimation Heuristics**:
*   **CPU**: Match independent tasks; defaults are 1 core (single-threaded), 8 (vectorised), or 16 (multi-process). Avoid oversubscription unless using OpenMP/MKL/joblib.
*   **Memory**: Tabular data requires ~3-5× input size; PyTorch needs 4 bytes/param + 8 bytes/param (Adam) + activations. Use `/usr/bin/time -v` for peak memory measurement.
*   **Wall Time**: Estimate 2-5× small-scale benchmarks plus 10% safety; schedulers kill jobs at the limit without warning.
*   **GPUs**: Request via `--gres=gpu:N` (SLURM) or equivalent; match model (A100/H100) to needs.

**SLURM Template Best Practices**:
*   Use `set -euo pipefail` for error handling.
*   Use `srun` inside `sbatch` for distributed tasks and signal propagation.
*   Use `--unbuffered` or `python -u` for real-time logging.
*   Use `/scratch` for fast I/O; stage data from network FS at start.
*   Pin thread counts (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, etc.) to requested CPUs.
*   Set reproducibility flags (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG`).

**Array Jobs**:
*   Submit single array jobs (e.g., `--array=0-479%50`) rather than multiple jobs to prevent filesystem thrashing.
*   PBS uses `$PBS_ARRAY_INDEX`; SGE uses `$SGE_TASK_ID`; LSF uses `$LSB_JOBINDEX`.

**Other Schedulers**:
*   **PBS**: Uses `#PBS -l select=...` for resources and `-m abe` for mail.
*   **SGE**: Uses `#$ -pe smp` for parallel environments and `#$ -l mem_free`.
*   **LSF**: Uses `#BSUB -n` for cores and `#BSUB -R` for resource requests.

**Workflow Engines**:
*   **Snakemake**: Use `--profile slurm` to handle partition, memory, and time via `resources`.
*   **Nextflow**: Configure `executor = 'slurm'` in `nextflow.config` with specific queues and limits.

**Containers**:
*   Prefer Apptainer/Singularity over host modules for reproducibility.
*   Use `--nv` for GPU access and `--bind` for path mounting.
*   Pin images by digest.

**Common Mistakes**:
*   Requesting more memory than available causes indefinite pending.
*   Underestimating wall time leads to job termination; overestimating increases queue wait.
*   Missing `srun` in distributed SLURM jobs results in single-rank execution.

knowledge/concepts/hybrid-search-keyword.title: Hybrid Search - Combining Keyword and Semantic Retrieval
knowledge/concepts/hybrid-search-keyword.description:
Hybrid search merges keyword and semantic retrieval to deliver unified ranked results that balance exact term matching with conceptual understanding.
It employs a three-stage process involving parallel retrieval, score normalization, and fusion via methods like Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
This technique is ideal for enterprise search systems where queries require both precise terminology matching and broad conceptual relevance.
Hybrid search matters because it overcomes the individual limitations of keyword-only and semantic-only approaches to reduce false negatives and irrelevant results.
knowledge/concepts/hybrid-search-keyword.summary: Hybrid search combines keyword search (BM25) and semantic search (vector embeddings) to deliver a unified ranked result set, addressing the limitations of each method used in isolation. The process involves three stages: parallel retrieval of top results from both systems, normalization of disparate scoring scales (BM25 vs. cosine similarity), and fusion via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) or weighted combination. While keyword search excels at exact matches like IDs and technical terms, semantic search captures conceptual meaning and synonyms; hybridization balances precision with understanding. Implementation patterns include weighted combination, RRF, and sequential filtering. Key benefits include up to 9% improved recall and robustness to query phrasing, though latency increases due to dual searches. Best practices involve testing weighting parameters, applying metadata filtering, implementing re-ranking, and monitoring performance to avoid fusion noise where pure vector search suffices.

knowledge/concepts/kg-summary-three-tier.title: KG-Summary Three-Tier Generation Pipeline
knowledge/concepts/kg-summary-three-tier.description: This pipeline automatically generates concise 2-3 sentence summaries for every knowledge graph node and stores them in a JSON file for retrieval clients. It intelligently selects backend models like local Ollama, Claude CLI, or OpenAI APIs based on availability and user consent. The system resolves node titles from YAML frontmatter or fallback headings to ensure malformed nodes still receive summaries. It matters because it enhances hybrid search capabilities while handling failures like timeouts and race conditions through sequential processing.
knowledge/concepts/kg-summary-three-tier.summary: The KG-Summary Three-Tier Generation Pipeline automatically generates 2-3 sentence summaries for knowledge graph nodes, triggered by `PostToolUse` hooks and stored in `knowledge/.node_formats.json` for retrieval. The system selects a backend in priority order: `claude` CLI (gated by authentication), Ollama (default local model `qwen3.5:9b`), OpenAI API (opt-in), Anthropic direct API, or silent skip, with configuration controlled by `KG_SUMMARY_BACKEND` and specific Ollama parameters. Title resolution prioritizes YAML frontmatter `title:` fields, falling back to the body H1 to prevent skipping malformed nodes, while missing titles result in node exclusion. The implementation addresses failure modes such as timeouts for large nodes, race conditions during parallel writes (resolved via sequential backfill), and cross-platform issues like Windows `PATHEXT` handling and environment variable separation between project and orchestrator roots.

knowledge/concepts/knowledge-graph.md.title: Knowledge Graph
knowledge/concepts/knowledge-graph.md.description:
A knowledge graph is a structured data model representing real-world entities and their relationships as nodes and edges.
It encodes semantic meaning directly in its structure to enable multi-hop reasoning and inference over interconnected facts.
This technology supports enterprise AI, RAG systems, and multi-agent coordination by providing explicit, typed relationships unlike flat document stores.
It matters because it allows complex queries and deep insights that relational databases and vector databases cannot natively support.
knowledge/concepts/knowledge-graph.md.summary: A knowledge graph is a structured data model representing real-world entities (nodes) and their semantic relationships (edges), enabling multi-hop reasoning and inference unlike flat document or vector stores. Core components include typed entities with properties, directed relationships carrying semantics, and schemas defining constraints via property graphs, RDF triples, or hybrid models. While relational databases offer ACID compliance and document stores provide flexibility, knowledge graphs excel at explicit relationships and complex queries despite higher schema complexity. Construction methods range from manual curation to LLM-powered extraction, with hybrid approaches offering the best quality-cost balance. In RAG systems, they enhance retrieval through graph traversal, community detection, and explainable, relationship-specific queries. This project utilizes Weaviate for storage, stores nodes as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, defines relationships via typed WikiLinks, and employs a hybrid search combining semantic and keyword methods using `qwen3-embedding:0.6b`.

knowledge/concepts/kubernetes-manifest-r.title: Kubernetes Manifest Review Discipline
knowledge/concepts/kubernetes-manifest-r.description:
This node defines a per-kind checklist for validating Kubernetes manifests against security and operational best practices.
It mandates explicit security contexts, balanced resource requests and limits, correct probe semantics, and proper disruption tolerances.
Engineers use this discipline to review pull requests and ensure deployed objects meet safety and stability standards.
It matters because it prevents insecure configurations, ensures predictable QoS classes, and maintains cluster isolation.
knowledge/concepts/kubernetes-manifest-r.summary:
**Kubernetes Manifest Review Discipline** defines a per-kind checklist distinct from the resource model, prioritizing security, correctness, and resilience. The review pyramid applies checks in this order: Security Context, Resource Correctness, Probes, Disruption Tolerance, and Network Exposure.

**1. Pod & Container Security Context**
*   **Principle:** Default deny. Every container must define a `securityContext`.
*   **Mandatory Settings:** `runAsNonRoot: true`, explicit `runAsUser` (not 0), `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, and `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault`.
*   **Pod-level:** Set `fsGroup` for volume ownership and `runAsNonRoot`.
*   **Red Flags:** `privileged: true`, `hostNetwork/PID/IPC: true`, `hostPath` volumes (must be `readOnly`), unnecessary capability additions, missing `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, and mutable image tags (`:latest`) without digests.

**2. Resource Requests & Limits**
*   **Requirements:** All containers need CPU/memory requests and memory limits.
*   **QoS Strategy:** Memory limits must equal requests to achieve **Guaranteed** QoS (safe from OOM-kill). Burstable is for non-critical workloads; BestEffort is for transient pods.
*   **CPU Limits:** Contested setting. Always setting prevents starvation but causes throttling; never setting allows saturation. Teams must pick a convention (e.g., limit untrusted workloads, omit for latency-sensitive first-party).

**3. Probes**
*   **Roles:** `startupProbe` handles slow starts (prevents restart loops); `livenessProbe` detects deadlocks (pod-local health only); `readinessProbe` manages traffic routing.
*   **Best Practices:** Use distinct endpoints for liveness and readiness. Use `startupProbe` with high `failureThreshold` for slow apps instead of relying solely on `initialDelaySeconds`. Tune `failureThreshold` based on app stability.

**4. Disruption Tolerance**
*   **Replicas/Strategy:** Use `maxUnavailable: 0` for zero-downtime rolling updates.
*   **PDB:** Use `PodDisruptionBudget` to guarantee availability during voluntary disruptions.
*   **Anti-Affinity:** Prefer `topologySpreadConstraints` over `podAntiAffinity` for spreading replicas across nodes/topologies.
*   **Termination:** Extend `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and use `preStop` hooks to drain connections before SIGTERM.

**5. Network Exposure**
*   **Policy:** Adopt default-deny ingress with explicit allow rules. Egress default-deny is harder but recommended for production.
*   **Services:** Prefer `ClusterIP` + Ingress over `LoadBalancer` for HTTP. Use `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` only if the external LB handles per-pod balancing.
*   **Compatibility:** Ensure the CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium) supports NetworkPolicy enforcement.

knowledge/concepts/kubernetes-resource-m.title: Kubernetes Resource Model — Requests, Limits, QoS Classes, and Eviction
knowledge/concepts/kubernetes-resource-m.description:
This Kubernetes resource model defines pod scheduling and eviction rules based on CPU and memory requests versus limits.
It establishes three Quality of Service classes—Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort—to prioritize pod survival during node pressure.
The system evicts pods in a specific order starting with BestEffort to protect critical workloads when resources are scarce.
Setting requests and limits correctly ensures that CPU throttling or memory OOM kills occur only when appropriate for the workload type.
knowledge/concepts/kubernetes-resource-m.summary: Kubernetes schedules and evicts pods based on CPU/memory **requests** (guaranteed capacity) and **limits** (usage ceiling). The combination of these values determines the **QoS class**: `Guaranteed` (request == limit for all containers), `Burstable` (at least one resource set but not Guaranteed), or `BestEffort` (no requests/limits). Under node pressure, the kubelet evicts pods in this order: `BestEffort`, then `Burstable` (prioritizing those exceeding requests), and finally `Guaranteed`. Critical workloads should use `Guaranteed` QoS with memory limits always set to prevent OOM kills, while CPU limits are often omitted for latency-sensitive services to avoid CFS throttling. Production-grade deployments must include `PodDisruptionBudgets`, `topologySpreadConstraints`, and three distinct health probes (`startup`, `liveness`, `readiness`) to ensure high availability and graceful degradation.

knowledge/concepts/launcher-paid-modules.title: Launcher Paid Modules — Supabase Schema (004_paid_modules.sql)
knowledge/concepts/launcher-paid-modules.description:
This schema extends the profiles table with a JSONB column to track user-owned add-on modules like Telegram or Discord.
It uses a flexible key-value structure to avoid database migrations when new modules are introduced.
A GIN index enables efficient querying of module entitlements while triggers prevent direct client writes.
The design supports Lemon Squeezy webhooks for purchase persistence and evolved runtime validation flows.
knowledge/concepts/launcher-paid-modules.summary: The `profiles.paid_modules` JSONB column in the Supabase `profiles` table tracks user-owned add-on modules (e.g., Telegram, Discord) using a flexible, GIN-indexed schema to avoid per-column migrations. While the original single-endpoint `validate-module` design utilizing this column is superseded by a three-endpoint architecture (`validate-tier`, `rl-artifact-url`, `module-catalog`) where entitlements of truth reside in `tier_cache.module_licenses`, the `paid_modules` column remains relevant for org-side persistence and Lemon Squeezy webhook integration. The schema includes triggers to prevent direct client writes, service-role RPCs (`upsert_paid_module`, `remove_paid_module`) for managing license metadata, and an `active_paid_modules` view for analytics. The commercial flow involves Lemon Squeezy webhooks populating the column on purchase, followed by launcher-side validation and installation, with deferred tasks including multi-machine enforcement and the deployment of the launcher-side `validate-module` endpoint.

knowledge/concepts/merchant-of-record-vs.title: Merchant of Record vs Stripe for Indies
knowledge/concepts/merchant-of-record-vs.description:
This node compares direct payment processors like Stripe with Merchant of Record services such as Lemon Squeezy for indie developers.
It highlights that MoRs assume legal liability for global sales tax, VAT, and chargebacks while direct processors require the seller to handle these obligations.
The primary use case involves solo founders deciding whether to pay a fee premium for tax compliance or manage filings themselves.
It matters because the choice fundamentally shifts operational focus from product building to regulatory compliance and financial risk management.
knowledge/concepts/merchant-of-record-vs.summary: For solo founders selling globally, the choice between a Direct Payment Processor (e.g., Stripe) and a Merchant of Record (MoR; e.g., Lemon Squeezy, Paddle, Polar) determines legal liability for sales tax, VAT, refunds, and chargebacks. While Stripe charges ~2.9% + fees and requires the founder to handle tax nexus registration and remittance, MoRs charge a premium (~5% + fees) but fully manage compliance, including EU VAT MOSS, US state sales tax, GDPR DPAs, and fraud handling. MoRs are the recommended default for global audiences, especially those under $5K MRR where the compliance cost exceeds the fee premium, or if selling to EU consumers to avoid quarterly filing burdens. Direct processors remain optimal for US-only B2B, needs for custom invoicing with the founder's name, or scaling beyond the ~$30-50K MRR crossover point where accounting costs outweigh MoR fees. Migration between providers is painful due to non-portable card data and subscription states, making the initial decision critical.

knowledge/concepts/model-context-protoco.title: Model Context Protocol
knowledge/concepts/model-context-protoco.description:
Model Context Protocol is an open standard by Anthropic that acts as a universal connector for AI models to access external data and tools.
It utilizes a client-server architecture to expose capabilities through tools, resources, and prompts via stdio or HTTP transports.
The protocol enables secure, explicit interactions where LLMs decide when to invoke functions while hosts control server access.
This matters because it replaces bespoke integrations with a stable, standardized interface for connecting AI to diverse data sources.
knowledge/concepts/model-context-protoco.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard by Anthropic that standardizes AI model connections to external data and tools, functioning as a universal connector. It utilizes a client-server architecture where hosts (e.g., Claude, VS Code) connect to servers exposing three core primitives: **tools** (executable functions called by the LLM), **resources** (URI-addressed data read by the host), and **prompts** (pre-defined templates). Transport mechanisms include stdio for local processes and HTTP/SSE for remote streaming. The protocol flow involves initialization, capability negotiation, and LLM-controlled tool invocation, while the security model ensures servers lack full conversation access and requires explicit user approval for dangerous operations. Implementation is supported by official Python and TypeScript SDKs, with FastMCP serving as a high-level Python framework. Key design decisions include stateless operations by default, JSON-RPC 2.0 as the underlying format, and a clear separation of concerns between tools, resources, and prompts.

knowledge/concepts/model-quantization.md.title: Model Quantization
knowledge/concepts/model-quantization.md.description:
Model quantization reduces numerical precision of neural network weights and activations to decrease memory footprint, accelerate inference, and lower power consumption.
It maps high-precision values like FP32 to lower-precision representations such as INT8 or INT4 to optimize transformer components like weights, activations, and KV cache.
The technique employs post-training quantization for quick deployment or quantization-aware training to recover accuracy during the training process.
Granularity levels ranging from per-tensor to per-group allow mixed-precision strategies that balance accuracy retention with computational overhead.
This optimization is essential for deploying large language models on resource-constrained devices and enabling long-context inference within limited memory budgets.
knowledge/concepts/model-quantization.md.summary: Model Quantization reduces neural network memory footprint and power consumption by mapping high-precision weights and activations to lower-precision formats (INT8, INT4, INT2). It targets three components: static model weights, dynamic activations requiring calibration, and KV caches critical for long-context inference. The two primary approaches are Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), which offers quick deployment with varying accuracy retention depending on the method (e.g., GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, bitsandbytes), and Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), which simulates quantization during training to recover accuracy but incurs significant compute overhead. Accuracy varies by granularity level (per-tensor to per-group) and is further optimized through mixed-precision strategies. Quantization is frequently combined with techniques like pruning, distillation, gradient checkpointing, and LoRA (QLoRA) to enhance compression and enable fine-tuning on consumer hardware.
