Performance and method suitability are highly dependent on hardware architecture, ranging from Tensor Core optimization on NVIDIA Ada GPUs to CPU-optimized GGUF formats. This technique is essential for multi-agent systems, allowing multiple models to run simultaneously within constrained VRAM environments.

knowledge/concepts/module-contributed-gu.title: Module-Contributed GUI Tabs Framework
knowledge/concepts/module-contributed-gu.description:
This framework allows installed modules to declare configuration tabs in a JSON manifest without bundling custom Svelte components or rebuilding the launcher.
Key features include zero extra builds per module, type-safe Rust validation of the manifest structure, and built-in mouseover tooltips for every control.
Paid and free module authors use it to expose settings in the launcher sidebar by defining a `gui.config_tab` block in their `vct-module.json`.
It matters because it enforces a secure Tauri security model by avoiding dynamic JS loads while providing a consistent, extensible UI palette.
knowledge/concepts/module-contributed-gu.summary: The Module-Contributed GUI Tabs Framework (v0.2.20+) allows installed modules to declare configuration tabs via a `gui.config_tab` JSON block in their manifest, enabling the launcher to render UI without bundling Svelte components or rebuilding the binary. This schema-rendered approach was chosen over webview-bundling or external executables to ensure zero extra builds, type safety, built-in tooltips, and adherence to Tauri security models. The framework supports five control kinds (Checkbox, MultiSelect, Button, Select, Info), each requiring a tooltip, with state persisted in a `module_settings` table keyed by project, module, and control ID. The launcher dynamically merges exposed tabs into the sidebar, soft-failing on broken manifests. Key evolutions include `show_in_sidebar: false` (v0.2.23) to support embedded tabs in per-project settings, scope refactoring of the orchestrator-core (v0.2.25), and a major schema expansion in v0.2.26 introducing a declarative dispatcher and new control kinds to accommodate future paid modules without requiring launcher rebuilds.

knowledge/concepts/motion-principles-for.title: Motion Principles for UI
knowledge/concepts/motion-principles-for.description:
Motion Principles for UI adapts Disney's animation rules to make interfaces feel alive and responsive rather than robotic.
Key features include answering four user questions about origin, destination, current state, and changes, plus using spring physics and easing curves.
Use cases involve guiding user attention, reducing uncertainty during loading, and providing visual feedback for state updates.
It matters because well-executed motion communicates context and intent while avoiding the slowdowns and disorientation caused by poor animation.
knowledge/concepts/motion-principles-for.summary: Motion in UI serves as a communication channel answering four core questions: origin, destination, current state, and recent changes. It adapts Disney's 12 animation principles by replacing character-specific techniques with UI constraints: squash and stretch becomes spring physics (avoiding text), anticipation becomes hover/loading states, staging ensures single focal points, and easing curves replace linear motion. Timing must adhere to specific durations (micro-interactions <200ms, page transitions 400-600ms), while exaggeration is minimized to preserve clarity. Accessibility is mandatory via `prefers-reduced-motion` media queries to prevent vestibular issues, and performance relies strictly on GPU-accelerated transform and opacity properties to maintain 60fps. Brands should define 3-5 signature motions (e.g., route transitions, modal opens) tokenized within the design system, avoiding decorative motion that conflicts with functional communication.

knowledge/concepts/neurosymbolic-ai.md.title: Neurosymbolic AI
knowledge/concepts/neurosymbolic-ai.md.description:
Neurosymbolic AI combines neural learning with symbolic reasoning to create interpretable systems that handle both unstructured data and logical constraints.
Key features include end-to-end differentiable unification of logic and perception, support for weighted model counting and fuzzy logic, and architectures like Logical Tensor Networks for knowledge-constrained learning.
Use cases span knowledge graph completion, multi-hop reasoning, and structured prediction where some facts come from perception while others follow domain logic.
This approach matters because it overcomes the individual limitations of neural networks and symbolic AI by enabling systematic generalization, transparency, and robustness to uncertainty.
knowledge/concepts/neurosymbolic-ai.md.summary: Neurosymbolic AI (NeSy) integrates neural network learning with symbolic reasoning to combine pattern recognition with transparency and systematic generalization. It is unified under a measure-theoretic formalism where logical satisfaction is weighted by neural belief functions. Key architectures include Logical Tensor Networks (LTN) for differentiable logic constraints, DeepProbLog for probabilistic inference with neural predicates, and Neural Logic Programming for knowledge graph reasoning. Architectures range from pipeline systems (Neuro→Symbolic) to tightly coupled end-to-end hybrids. Recent progress focuses on integrating Large Language Models with symbolic tools for verification, program synthesis, and handling structured tasks like math reasoning and autonomous driving, addressing limitations in scalability, discrete gradient flow, and rule discovery.

knowledge/concepts/oauth2-flow-decision-.title: OAuth2 Flow Decision Tree
knowledge/concepts/oauth2-flow-decision-.description:
It is a decision framework for selecting the correct OAuth2 authentication flow based on resource ownership and client environment.
Key features include distinguishing between user-delegated and service-to-service access scenarios.
It mandates the use of modern standards like Authorization Code with PKCE for all user-facing applications.
The primary use case is guiding developers to avoid architectural rewrites by choosing the right flow during initial API integration.
It matters because selecting the wrong flow compromises security or forces costly system changes later.
knowledge/concepts/oauth2-flow-decision-.summary: The OAuth2 flow selection depends on whether access is delegated by an end user or performed by the application itself, and the environment where the client runs. For user-delegated access, server-side apps use Authorization Code with PKCE (optionally with a secret), while SPAs/mobile apps use Authorization Code with PKCE (no secret, mandatory PKCE), and CLIs/IoT devices use the Device Authorization Grant. Long-lived offline access requires the `offline_access` scope and secure refresh token storage. For service-to-service flows, use the Client Credentials Grant (storing secrets in a secret manager) or platform-native workload identities (AWS IAM, GCP Workload Identity, Azure Managed Identity) instead of static credentials. The JWT Bearer flow is used for service accounts impersonating users. Critical anti-patterns include storing client secrets in client-side code, using deprecated Implicit or Resource Owner Password Credentials flows, hard-coding tokens without refresh logic, and sharing refresh tokens across users. Access tokens should be cached in memory, refresh tokens encrypted at rest with per-user keys, and client secrets managed via secret managers. Always request least-privilege scopes and re-prompt for new permissions.

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-code-gra.title: Orchestrator Code Graph
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-code-gra.description:
It is a semantic index of source code that extracts structural entities and stores them in Weaviate for both semantic and structural queries.
Key features include finding code by purpose rather than exact strings, answering structural questions without reading files, and supporting incremental analysis of changed files.
Use cases involve locating authentication middleware or database retry logic by their function and identifying callers of specific functions or module imports.
It matters because it enables developers to navigate complex codebases efficiently by understanding code relationships and intent instead of relying on traditional grep searches.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-code-gra.summary: The Orchestrator Code Graph is a semantic index of source code that extracts structural entities (modules, classes, functions, APIs, interactions), embeds them using specialized models (CodeSage-Large-v2 on GPU or Jina on CPU), and stores them in Weaviate for both semantic and structural queries. It enables purpose-based code discovery and answers structural questions like identifying callers or dependencies without reading files. The analysis pipeline supports language detection, AST parsing for Python, regex extraction for others, and incremental updates via `git diff` to re-analyze only changed files. Entities are stored in per-project Weaviate collections with named vectors to support backend switching. The system integrates via an MCP server for search and structure queries, a hook system that queues analysis after file edits, and a pre-edit hook that injects relevant code context.

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-context-.title: Orchestrator Context Management
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-context-.description:
Orchestrator Context Management preserves Claude's working state across compaction events using a two-layer memory architecture.
It maintains stable project facts in a local MEMORY.md file and active task details in a git-tracked CONTEXT_STATE.md file.
This system prevents loss of active task states, modified files, and plans when conversations are automatically summarized.
It utilizes RL-scored tiered injection and Lost-In-The-Middle ordering to reinject critical information at optimal positions.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-context-.summary: Orchestrator Context Management preserves Claude's working state across compaction events using a two-layer memory architecture and a save/restore pipeline. Layer 1 (`MEMORY.md`) stores stable, auto-loaded project facts (first 200 lines) locally, while Layer 2 (`CONTEXT_STATE.md`) holds active task state, blockers, and next steps in git (target 250-350 lines). The system employs a Pre-Compact Save Cycle to snapshot state before auto-compaction and a Post-Compact Reinject process using Lost-In-The-Middle (LITM) ordering to place critical information at the start and end of the reinjected payload. Session-level deduplication prevents context bloat by tracking injected nodes, and diff-based injection reduces token overhead by transmitting only changed sections after the initial prompt. Additional efficiency strategies include parallel tool calls, targeted file reads, agent delegation for multi-file tasks, and local analysis without external MCPs.

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-hook-sys.title: Orchestrator Hook System
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-hook-sys.description:
The Orchestrator Hook System acts as the orchestrator's nervous system by intercepting Claude Code lifecycle events to automate workflows with built-in security and context management.
Key features include blocking hooks that can abort operations, non-blocking background hooks for fire-and-forget tasks, and support for approximately 20 distinct lifecycle events.
Use cases involve enforcing security scans before tool execution, automatically syncing knowledge graphs, preserving context during compaction, and tracking session costs.
This system matters because it transforms a standard coding agent into a robust, self-managing workflow engine capable of quality gating and developer experience enhancements.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-hook-sys.summary:
The Orchestrator Hook System acts as the orchestrator's nervous system, intercepting Claude Code lifecycle events to enable autonomous workflows, security enforcement, knowledge-graph synchronization, cost tracking, and context preservation. Implemented as shell scripts (with Python helpers) in `.claude/settings.json`, hooks bind to ~20 lifecycle events and are categorized as blocking (aborting operations) or non-blocking (background execution).

**Core Functions:**
*   **Security:** Scans commands for shell injection, SSRF, and credential leaks; blocks unauthorized internal network access.
*   **Knowledge Sync:** Automatically pushes edited files to Weaviate and injects relevant context before tool use or edits.
*   **Context Management:** Saves state before compaction and reinjects critical info (CONTEXT_STATE.md, plans, snapshots) to prevent "Lost-In-The-Middle" issues, achieving 70-90% token savings via diff-based context injection.
*   **Quality & Cost:** Validates agent output, tracks token usage/costs, and manages container health (Podman/Docker).

**Architecture & Flow:**
1.  **SessionStart:** Initializes services, checks container health, surfaces embedding failures, and manages context size.
2.  **PreCompact:** Saves git status and recent file changes to snapshots.
3.  **PostCompact:** Logs events and sends notifications.
4.  **UserPromptSubmit:** Injects reminders, diffs, and skill suggestions.
5.  **PreToolUse:** Executes security guards (SSRF, shell injection) and injects KG context.
6.  **PostToolUse:** Syncs knowledge graphs and performs linting/type-checking.
7.  **Subagent Hooks:** Manage subagent spawning (KG injection) and stopping (output reconciliation).

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-knowledg.title: Orchestrator Knowledge Graph
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-knowledg.description:
The Orchestrator Knowledge Graph acts as the system's long-term memory by storing cross-project patterns and architectural decisions in Obsidian-style markdown files.
It automatically synchronizes content to a Weaviate vector database to enable semantic search for both human editors and AI clients.
The system enforces a "write once, search everywhere" principle to prevent future sessions from rediscovering known architectural ground.
Its folder structure organizes nodes into categories like projects, concepts, tools, and research while using typed wiki links to maintain an acyclic graph.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-knowledg.summary: The Orchestrator Knowledge Graph (KG) functions as the system's long-term memory, storing cross-project patterns, architectural decisions, and research as Obsidian-style markdown files synchronized to a Weaviate vector database via Ollama. It serves dual audiences: humans browse/edit files in the `knowledge/` directory, while AI clients (e.g., Claude) utilize MCP tools (`hybrid_search`, `semantic_graph_search`) for semantic and graph-based retrieval. Each node is a `.md` file with required YAML frontmatter (title, type, tags, dates, status) and optional temporal validity markers. Nodes utilize typed WikiLinks (e.g., `[[uses::Tool]]`) to define unidirectional relationships, maintaining an acyclic graph structure. The `knowledge/` directory is organized into subfolders for projects, concepts, tools, models, hardware, research, and coordination, supported by global files for tag hierarchy and vocabulary. A `PostToolUse` hook triggers an automated sync pipeline that parses frontmatter, extracts links, chunks content, embeds text using Ollama, and upserts data to Weaviate (skipping duplicates). The Weaviate schema supports temporal filtering (`indexNullState=True`) and named vectors for embedding migration resilience. Search capabilities include CLI keyword search and MCP semantic search (combining BM25 and vector similarity) with optional RL reranking and graph traversal. Programmatic writes are handled by the `store_knowledge_node` MCP tool, which resolves file paths relative to `KG_BASE_DIR` or the project root. Maintenance scripts perform integrity checks for broken links, missing frontmatter, and orphaned nodes.

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-mcp-serv.title: Orchestrator MCP Servers
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-mcp-serv.description:
Orchestrator MCP Servers are native Python processes that extend Claude Code with specialized semantic and academic search capabilities.
They manage knowledge graphs, code structures, and development documentation using Weaviate and Ollama infrastructure.
The system provides hybrid search tools that combine keyword and vector similarity across project-specific and shared collections.
These servers matter because they enable deep, context-aware retrieval for code and research without duplicating Claude's native reasoning abilities.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-mcp-serv.summary: The Orchestrator extends Claude Code with native MCP servers running in a shared virtual environment (`claude_mcp_servers/.venv`) to enable semantic search, academic paper retrieval, and code analysis. The primary server, `weaviate-kg`, manages the Knowledge Graph, Code Graph, and development documentation in Weaviate, offering tools for hybrid search (BM25 + vector fusion), graph traversal (GraphRAG), and code structure queries. A secondary `search` server handles structured academic paper retrieval via OpenAlex and arXiv. Supporting infrastructure includes a non-MCP FastAPI code-embedding service (port 11440) and Ollama, which provides text embeddings and CPU fallbacks but is not exposed as an MCP tool due to Claude's native capabilities covering chat, reading, and vision. Project-specific routing is managed via environment variables in `~/.claude.json`, ensuring the active workspace determines the active Knowledge Graph collections.

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-rl-retri.title: Orchestrator RL Retrieval
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-rl-retri.description:
Orchestrator RL Retrieval is a Pro-tier feature that wraps Weaviate searches with a reinforcement-learning reranking layer to improve result relevance.
It enables per-project deployment with isolated neural network states to prevent cross-project data leakage and mode collapse.
The system supports continuous online training after each search and includes strict license-gate behaviors that disable the feature on free tiers.
This matters because it provides a persistent competitive moat against piracy through weekly model-weight rotation and secure artifact distribution.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-rl-retri.summary: Orchestrator RL Retrieval is a Pro-tier feature that enhances Weaviate hybrid search with a reinforcement-learning (RL) reranking layer. The system over-fetches candidates from Weaviate, reranks them via a project-specific RL server based on learned relevance signals, and returns the top results. Online training continuously improves the model using call-sequence data as implicit feedback. Each project runs an isolated RL server instance to prevent cross-project data leakage, with ports allocated dynamically and managed via systemd units. Access is gated by license validation; free-tier users or those with offline licenses bypass the RL server, falling back to standard Weaviate ranking. The RL server uses a specific model architecture (SharedEncoder to MLP with Sigmoid) and supports graceful degradation if unavailable. The pipeline employs a 2x over-fetch ratio, tracks session call sequences for implicit rewards, and includes session-level deduplication to prevent context bloat. Model weights are distributed via short-lived pull tokens with weekly rotation to prevent piracy, and users can choose to fine-tune the model upon detecting new global weights.

knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-security.title: Orchestrator Security Model
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-security.description:
The Orchestrator Security Model is an automated defense-in-depth framework that enforces security rules via hooks without user intervention.
It operates through seven distinct layers targeting specific threats like credential leakage, SSRF, and shell injection.
Most layers function as pre-use blockers or post-use detectors to ensure failing one layer does not compromise overall security.
This system matters because it prevents common attack vectors such as environment variable exfiltration and blind file overwrites.
knowledge/concepts/orchestrator-security.summary: The Orchestrator implements an automated, defense-in-depth security model using seven distinct layers enforced by PreToolUse (blocking) and PostToolUse (detection) hooks. Layer 1 scrubs sensitive environment variables from subprocesses. Layer 2 blocks Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) by filtering internal/private IP ranges and cloud metadata endpoints, while whitelisting specific localhost services. Layer 3 scans for shell injection patterns (e.g., pipe-to-shell, eval) and destructive commands using regex rules. Layer 4 enforces a Build Anchor Protocol, preventing blind file overwrites of existing files not read in the current session. Layer 5 creates time-limited backups of files before modification to enable recovery. Layer 6 performs non-blocking detection of hardcoded credentials in written files, logging findings and notifying the user without halting operations. Layer 7 manages tool permissions via a declarative allow/deny list in settings. Blocking hooks exit with code 2 and surface explanations to the user, while all events are logged to specific security and failure directories.

knowledge/concepts/parallel-agent-worktr.title: Parallel-agent worktree isolation discipline
knowledge/concepts/parallel-agent-worktr.description:
This discipline mandates that parallel subagents operate in physically separate git worktrees to prevent concurrent commit conflicts.
Key features include enforcing distinct checkout directories, verifying isolation via prompt boilerplate, and auditing worktree counts before and after dispatch.
Use cases involve orchestrating multiple agents to modify codebases simultaneously without corrupting shared state or forcing complex merges.
It matters because it eliminates the need for costly cherry-picks and force resets when agents accidentally commit to the parent repository.
knowledge/concepts/parallel-agent-worktr.summary: When dispatching multiple Claude Code subagents in parallel via the `isolation: worktree` directive, every agent must operate in a physically separate git worktree for its entire run to prevent concurrent `git commit`/`checkout` conflicts. While the harness typically enforces this by creating isolated worktrees, agents can defeat isolation by changing directories to the parent checkout mid-session. To prevent this, a three-layer defense is required: (1) Trust the harness's default isolation and verify the agent's current working directory (CWD) and worktree list early; (2) Include a mandatory "verify-or-abort" prompt block that asserts the CWD is not the parent directory and forces creation of a new worktree if assertions fail; and (3) Perform pre/post-dispatch audits in the parent process to validate worktree counts and branch existence. This rule specifically addresses concurrent write contention, distinct from stale-base-SHA confusion bugs, and applies to all parallel-dispatch scenarios involving commits.

knowledge/concepts/physical-constants-qu.title: Physical Constants Quick Reference
knowledge/concepts/physical-constants-qu.description:
This node provides a curated list of canonical physical constants and useful combinations accurate to 5-6 significant figures for order-of-magnitude work.
It features exact SI redefined values alongside approximate masses and includes memorized combinations like thermal energy and rest mass energies.
The primary use case is performing quick sanity checks and order-of-magnitude estimations within the Equation Verification Methodology.
It matters because it enables rapid, publication-ready precision checks without needing to fetch external CODATA values for every calculation.
knowledge/concepts/physical-constants-qu.summary: This node provides a quick reference for canonical physical constants based on CODATA 2022 recommendations, accurate to 5-6 significant figures for order-of-magnitude checks and sanity verification. It lists SI constants (e.g., speed of light, Planck constant, Boltzmann constant) and particle masses, alongside useful derived combinations like thermal energy at room temperature ($k_B T \approx 25.85$ meV), rest energies ($m_e c^2 \approx 0.511$ MeV), and photon energy-wavelength relations ($hc \approx 1240$ eV·nm). The content includes a conversion cheat sheet for units such as eV, kcal/mol, and Hartree, astronomical constants (AU, Solar mass, Hubble constant), and guidance to prioritize library values from `scipy.constants` or `astropy.constants` over hardcoded numbers in production code.

knowledge/concepts/postmortem-authoring-.title: Postmortem Authoring Discipline
knowledge/concepts/postmortem-authoring-.description:
This discipline defines the authoring standards for post-mortems to ensure documents drive future behavioral change rather than gathering dust.
It mandates a UTC-timestamped timeline spine that distinguishes observations from actions and includes dead ends as evidence.
The approach replaces single-point root causes with a contributing-factor analysis to capture the systemic intersections that caused an outage.
It enforces concrete, unowned action items that remain understandable to new engineers a year later to prevent recurring failures.
knowledge/concepts/postmortem-authoring-.summary:
The Postmortem Authoring Discipline defines the standards for writing blameless incident reports that drive behavioral change rather than gathering dust. The core objective is to produce a document where action items are concrete enough for a new engineer to understand the changes and rationale one year later.

**Key Principles & Structure:**
*   **Timeline Reconstruction:** The document must be built on a spine of UTC timestamps derived from system data (not memory), distinguishing between observations and actions, and explicitly including dead ends as evidence of monitoring gaps.
*   **Contributing-Factor Analysis:** Outages are treated as intersections of multiple factors rather than a single "root cause." Analysis must stop at system/process levels (never individuals) and utilize the "5 Whys" technique to uncover systemic gaps.
*   **Action-Item Categorization:** Items must be categorized by intervention point: **Prevent** (stop recurrence), **Detect** (sooner notice), **Mitigate** (reduce blast radius), or **Document** (update runbooks). A healthy report includes items in at least three categories. Each item requires a specific named owner, a concrete due date, and verifiable exit criteria.
*   **Required Sections:** The document must follow a specific order: Summary, Impact (quantified), Timeline, Contributing Factors, What Went Well, What Went Poorly, Where We Got Lucky, Action Items, and Supporting Data.

**Anti-Patterns to Avoid:**
*   Blaming individuals or citing a single root cause.
*   Using vague, future-tense lessons ("be more careful") instead of specific, trackable tasks.
*   Omitting customer impact or lucky breaks that could become future failure points.
*   Creating unowned or unmeasured action items.

knowledge/concepts/power-analysis-sample.title: Power Analysis and Sample Size Estimation
knowledge/concepts/power-analysis-sample.description: This node provides formulas and tools for calculating required sample sizes and detecting minimum effects in study designs. It requires inputs like the smallest effect of interest, variability estimates, significance thresholds, and power targets. Researchers use it to prevent wasted resources and ensure studies can detect meaningful benefits. It matters because underpowered studies expose subjects to risk without the ability to detect true effects.
knowledge/concepts/power-analysis-sample.summary: Power analysis determines required sample sizes *a priori* or minimum detectable effects *post hoc* to avoid wasting resources or exposing subjects to risk without benefit. Essential inputs include the Smallest Effect of Scientific Interest (SESOI), variability estimate (pooled SD), significance threshold ($\alpha$, adjusted for multiple comparisons), power target ($1-\beta$, typically 0.80), and test type. For two independent groups with continuous outcomes, the rule-of-thumb is $n \approx 16/d^2$ (where $d$ is Cohen's $d$), while paired designs reduce required subjects by a factor of $(1-\rho)$ based on correlation. Survival analysis relies on Schoenfeld's formula for the number of events rather than subjects. Closed-form approximations fail for mixed-effects, longitudinal, adaptive, or complex multiple-comparison structures, necessitating Monte Carlo simulation. Critical failure modes include calculating meaningless post-hoc power, overestimating effects from literature without accounting for bias, powering for secondary outcomes, ignoring dropout rates, and confusing subjects with events. If sample sizes are infeasible, researchers should increase precision, widen the SESOI, adjust $\alpha$ (with preregistration), switch to Bayesian methods, or abandon the hypothesis. Recommended tools include Python's `statsmodels` and `lifelines`, R's `pwr`, `pwrss`, and `simr`, and standalone software like G*Power.

knowledge/concepts/ppo-improvements-st-p.title: PPO Improvements - SORL and Modern Variants
knowledge/concepts/ppo-improvements-st-p.description:
SORL stabilizes PPO training for multi-turn LLM agents by addressing token-level granularity mismatches and off-policy critic errors.
It employs turn-level importance sampling to aggregate credit across logical steps rather than individual tokens.
The method uses clipping-triggered normalization to correct bias introduced when standard clipping zeros out gradients.
SORL variants like SO-PPO and SO-GRPO prevent training collapse on complex reasoning tasks requiring long-horizon planning.
knowledge/concepts/ppo-improvements-st-p.summary: SORL (Stabilizing Off-policy Reinforcement Learning) addresses PPO instability in multi-turn LLM agents by combining turn-level importance sampling with clipping-triggered normalization. The solution resolves two root causes: granularity mismatch (token-level noise vs. turn-level credit) and off-policy critic errors (high-variance advantage estimates). SO-PPO retains a critic, while SO-GRPO is critic-free. Experimental results show SO-PPO achieves 85% success on multi-turn search tasks compared to 20% for standard token-level PPO, with significantly reduced gradient spikes and conservative clipping ratios. Key hyperparameters include a clip ratio of 0.2 and specific GAE settings. Related variants include TOPR, LUFFY, and GSPO, while SORL is recommended specifically for multi-turn reasoning and language modeling scenarios.

knowledge/concepts/process-reward-models.title: Process Reward Models
knowledge/concepts/process-reward-models.description:
Process Reward Models evaluate intermediate reasoning steps rather than just final answers to provide dense supervision signals.
They enable precise error localization mid-reasoning, preventing models from relying on spurious shortcuts that yield correct final answers.
PRMs are used in RL training and search algorithms to improve robustness on complex tasks like mathematical problem solving.
This approach matters because it offers cleaner training signals that foster genuine competence over outcome-based luck.
knowledge/concepts/process-reward-models.summary: Process Reward Models (PRMs) evaluate intermediate reasoning steps rather than just final answers, offering dense, step-level supervision that enables error localization and correction mid-reasoning. Unlike Outcome Reward Models (ORMs), which suffer from sparse signals and vulnerability to "correct answer, wrong reasoning" shortcuts, PRMs provide cleaner training signals for genuine competence but require richer, more expensive data. Key methodologies include human annotation (gold standard), Monte Carlo estimation (inferior due to conflating reachability with validity), LLM-as-a-judge, and consensus filtering. PRMs are central to training reasoning models (e.g., o1, DeepSeek-R1) and enable efficient inference scaling via Best-of-N search and beam pruning, significantly outperforming ORMs on benchmarks like MATH. Current limitations include high data acquisition costs, performance degradation on long chains, and poor cross-domain generalization.

knowledge/concepts/project-extra-codegra.title: Project-extra codegraph paths
knowledge/concepts/project-extra-codegra.description:
This feature allows indexing additional read-only filesystem paths into a project's codegraph without converting them into launcher projects.
It supports six launcher commands to manage extra paths while preventing unintended state changes like creating `.claude/` directories.
The system ensures accurate search results by unioning file UUIDs from primary repos and extras in a single pass during analysis.
It matters because it enables users to query sibling repositories or private forks without registering them as write targets or managing their own project state.
knowledge/concepts/project-extra-codegra.summary: The "Project-extra codegraph paths" feature allows indexing additional read-only filesystem paths into a project's codegraph collection without registering them as launcher projects. This architecture consists of four layers: a database table (`project_codegraph_extra_paths`) for persistence, a Tauri launcher with commands to manage paths and handle disambiguation when paths conflict with existing projects, a hub resolver API for configuration, and a GUI for user interaction. A critical invariant ensures that `--prune-stale` operations visit all relevant files in a single invocation to prevent UUID deletion conflicts, enforced via a per-project mutex and a shared set in the analyzer. Path canonicalization rules standardize paths before storage, while hook execution follows a first-match-wins order (own-repo → extras → siblings). The system supports audit logging for all state transitions and is designed to be backwards compatible, excluding knowledge graphs, diagrams, and write operations for these extra paths.

knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-fu.title: Prompt Engineering — Fundamentals (2026)
knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-fu.description:
This node outlines foundational prompting patterns for modern LLMs including Claude 4.x, GPT-4, and Gemini.
It emphasizes three core pillars: providing context, ensuring instruction clarity, and defining strict constraints.
Key techniques highlighted include Chain-of-Thought, few-shot learning, and role-based prompting to reduce errors.
The content is essential for developers needing to adapt to explicit instruction styles in newer model versions.
knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-fu.summary:
Effective prompting relies on three pillars: **Context provision**, **Instruction clarity**, and **Constraint definition**. Key empirical techniques include Chain-of-Thought (reducing reasoning errors by ~60%), Few-Shot Learning (3-5 examples optimal), and Role-Based prompting (improving domain accuracy by 20-40%).

**Claude 4.x** requires explicit instructions over implicit ones, demands stated motivation, leverages built-in reflection, and defaults to literal task execution unless "above and beyond" behavior is requested.

**Fundamental rules** dictate clarity, simplicity (one task per prompt), and iterative refinement. **Model parameters** should be tuned based on task type: low temperature/top-p for deterministic code, moderate for documentation, and high for creativity. **Advanced techniques** include Self-Consistency for critical decisions and Meta-prompting to generate optimal prompts. **Model-specific strategies** involve high-level guidance for reasoning models, precise step-by-step instructions for GPTs, and balanced instruction with motivation for Claude 4.x.

knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-mc.title: Prompt Engineering — MCP and Tool Design (2026)
knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-mc.description:
This node defines prompt engineering standards for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) used by major AI companies to connect LLMs with tools, resources, and prompts.
It distinguishes three orthogonal capabilities: tools for function calls, prompts for parameterized instructions, and resources for read-only data retrieval.
Effective design requires verb-first tool names, inline trigger conditions, and limiting the tool list to 10–15 items to maintain selection accuracy.
The knowledge matters for production security and reliable multi-agent systems where models must decide when and how to invoke external functions.
knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-mc.summary: MCP standardizes LLM tool integration via three orthogonal capabilities: Tools (function calls requiring decision logic), Prompts (parameterized instruction templates), and Resources (URI-addressable read-only data). Effective design requires distinct prompt shapes for each: Tools need signatures, descriptions, trigger conditions, and return shapes; Prompts require typed arguments with sane defaults and declared output formats; Resources need URI schemes, templated parameters, and bounded fetch lists. Security hardening mandates input validation, least-privilege permission tiers (READ-ONLY, READ-DATA, WRITE, ADMIN), treating external content as untrusted data rather than instructions, and logging all invocations. Best practices include using verb-first tool names, limiting tool counts to 10–15, avoiding disabled tools, and grouping rare tools into meta-tools to prevent selection degradation.

knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-mu.title: Prompt Engineering — Multi-Agent (2026)
knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-mu.description:
This node defines prompt patterns for orchestrating multiple LLM agents to collaborate on complex tasks.
It supports parallel specialist work, iterative refinement, and lateral communication between agents.
Use it for domains requiring diverse expertise where simple single-agent prompts would regress quality.
It matters because it enables distributed planning loops and system contracts that prevent coordination overhead from slowing simple linear tasks.
knowledge/concepts/prompt-engineering-mu.summary: Multi-agent systems utilize specialized LLM agents (orchestrators and specialists) to handle complex, parallelizable tasks requiring iterative refinement, avoiding them for simple or low-latency scenarios. Coordination follows three topologies: **Orchestration** (a central agent delegates and synthesizes), **Agent-to-Agent (A2A)** (specialists share findings via a shared protocol like `[BROADCAST]`), and **Distributed Planning** (agents maintain independent goals/states). Effective prompts use a "shared-context-then-agent-specific" structure where the system prompt acts as a short contract defining Role, Goal, Constraints, Uncertainty Handling, Output Format, Tools, and Success Criteria. Model selection stratifies costs by assigning premium models to high-weight decision roles, balanced models to planning/coding, and cheap models to validation/routing. Key anti-patterns include overloaded orchestrators, echo chambers, implicit handoffs, scope creep, and unresolved disagreements, all mitigated by strict delegation, cross-agent broadcasting, defined schemas, and explicit decision criteria.

knowledge/concepts/qlora.md.title: QLoRA
knowledge/concepts/qlora.md.description:
QLoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that combines 4-bit quantization with Low-Rank Adaptation to train large models on consumer hardware.
It freezes base model weights in 4-bit NormalFloat format while training small adapter matrices in 16-bit precision to drastically reduce VRAM usage.
The method enables fine-tuning massive 65B+ parameter models on a single 48GB GPU by utilizing paged optimizers and double quantization for stability.
This approach allows developers to adapt state-of-the-art LLMs without requiring enterprise-grade data centers or multi-GPU clusters.
knowledge/concepts/qlora.md.summary: QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method introduced by Dettmers et al. (NeurIPS 2023) that enables fine-tuning of large LLMs (65B+ parameters) on consumer hardware (single GPU with 48GB VRAM) by combining 4-bit quantization of frozen base model weights with 16-bit trained LoRA adapters. It utilizes NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat) quantization optimized for normally distributed weights, double quantization to save ~0.37 bits/parameter, and paged optimizers to manage VRAM via CPU offloading. The method reduces VRAM requirements significantly (e.g., ~48 GB for a 65B model vs. ~1040 GB for full fine-tuning) while maintaining quality within 1–2% of full fine-tuning for instruction following and chat tasks, though it may underperform on low-resource languages or highly specialized domains. Implementation relies on `bitsandbytes` for quantization and `PEFT` for adapter injection, with recommended hyperparameters including rank (r) of 8–64, alpha of 2×r, and learning rates of 2e-4 to 3e-4.

knowledge/concepts/raft-consensus-algori.title: Raft Consensus Algorithm
knowledge/concepts/raft-consensus-algori.description:
Raft is a distributed consensus algorithm that ensures replicated state machines agree on a sequence of operations through leader election and log replication.
It decomposes consensus into independent subproblems of leader election, log replication, and safety to achieve understandability unlike Paxos.
The algorithm relies on randomized election timeouts, majority quorums, and strict log matching to prevent split votes and maintain data consistency.
It is widely used in distributed systems like etcd and Consul to provide reliable fault tolerance without Byzantine fault tolerance guarantees.
This matters because it offers a formally proven, simpler alternative to Paxos that is easier to implement and reason about for building robust distributed services.
knowledge/concepts/raft-consensus-algori.summary: Raft is a crash fault-tolerant consensus algorithm introduced in 2014 to provide an understandable alternative to Paxos by decomposing consensus into three independent subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety. It operates with a single leader, followers, and candidates, utilizing randomized election timeouts and term-based logical clocks to ensure at most one leader per term. Consensus is achieved when a majority of nodes acknowledge a log entry, after which the leader applies the state and returns results to clients. Raft handles cluster reconfiguration via joint consensus to maintain quorum during membership changes. While it offers strong linearizability and simpler operational models than Paxos, it has a single leader bottleneck, lacks Byzantine fault tolerance, and requires careful handling of log gaps during leader failover. Notable implementations include etcd, CockroachDB, and TiKV.

knowledge/concepts/rag-pattern.md.title: RAG Pattern
knowledge/concepts/rag-pattern.md.description:
The RAG Pattern is an architectural approach for LLM applications that grounds responses in external documents instead of relying solely on model weights.
It decouples knowledge bases from models to enable cheap updates without expensive retraining or fine-tuning.
This pattern is essential for domains requiring factual precision, traceable sources, and frequent knowledge changes.
Variants like Iterative and Fusion RAG extend the core concept to handle complex multi-step questions and reduce retrieval bias.
knowledge/concepts/rag-pattern.md.summary: The RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Pattern is an architectural solution for LLM applications requiring access to dynamic, private, or domain-specific knowledge. It decouples the knowledge base from the model to enable cheap updates without retraining. The core intent is to ground responses in retrieved documents rather than relying solely on parametric weights, addressing limitations like static knowledge cutoffs and hallucination. The standard structure involves embedding documents into a vector store, retrieving top-k results for a query, building a prompt, and generating a final answer via an LLM. Key variants include Standard (single retrieval), Iterative (multi-round with reasoning), Fusion (query expansion), Corrective (quality evaluation with fallback), and Speculative (parallel verification). Critical implementation practices include managing chunk overlap (10–20%), filtering metadata, using re-ranking, ensuring context fits the window, tracking citations, and caching embeddings. Common anti-patterns involve improper chunk sizing, stale indices, and mismatched embedding models.

knowledge/concepts/read-image-memory-awa.title: read_image — Memory-Aware Vision-Model Gating
knowledge/concepts/read-image-memory-awa.description:
This node implements memory-aware gating logic for the read_image MCP tool to select appropriate vision models based on available system resources.
It features per-model VRAM and RAM thresholds, a tiered resize budget clamped to hardware limits, and automatic fallback to smaller models when resources are constrained.
The use case involves invoking the opt-in read_image tool against a running Ollama instance to retrieve base64 image data with optional on-device descriptions.
It matters because it prevents out-of-memory crashes by conservatively probing system capabilities and ensuring functional image processing within existing hardware limits.
knowledge/concepts/read-image-memory-awa.summary: The `read_image` MCP tool provides memory-aware vision-model gating for Ollama, returning images as base64 data URLs while optionally running on-device vision models. It probes free VRAM and system RAM at module load to select a model, clamp image resolution, or skip description generation. Per-model thresholds define VRAM/RAM floors for qwen3.5 (4b–9b), llama3.2-vision (11b/90b), and gemma3/4 models. The system auto-fallbacks to smaller installed models if the preferred one exceeds memory limits, or skips the description if no model fits, always ensuring the base64 image is returned for Claude. Resolution is clamped based on free VRAM tiers (256² to 1024² pixels) to prevent context waste. This design prevents OOM errors and silent hangs by providing clear skip reasons and graceful degradation.

knowledge/concepts/reinforcement-learnin.title: Reinforcement Learning
knowledge/concepts/reinforcement-learnin.description:
Reinforcement Learning is a machine learning paradigm where an agent learns optimal decision-making by interacting with an environment to maximize cumulative rewards.
It operates through a core loop of observing states, selecting actions, receiving feedback, and updating its policy to improve future outcomes.
The field balances exploration of new actions against exploitation of known high-reward strategies using techniques like epsilon-greedy or Upper Confidence Bound.
Major algorithm categories include value-based methods like Q-Learning, policy gradient approaches like PPO, and actor-critic hybrids that combine both strategies.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a critical application that aligns large language models with human preferences through iterative reward modeling.
knowledge/concepts/reinforcement-learnin.summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm where an agent learns to maximize cumulative reward by interacting with an environment through a loop of observation, action, transition, and feedback. Core components include the agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy, and value functions. Agents balance exploration (trying new actions) and exploitation (using known high-reward actions), often using strategies like ε-greedy or UCB. RL algorithms are categorized into value-based methods (e.g., Q-Learning, DQN), policy gradient methods (e.g., REINFORCE, PPO), and actor-critic methods that combine both. In Large Language Models, RLHF aligns models via supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, and RL optimization (PPO/GRPO). RL is also applied to agent routing to optimize query handling based on success and cost. Key challenges include sample inefficiency, sparse rewards, credit assignment, training instability, and reward hacking.

knowledge/concepts/reproducible-research.title: Reproducible Research Workflows
knowledge/concepts/reproducible-research.description:
Reproducible Research Workflows ensure third parties can recover identical outputs from the same inputs, code, and environment.
Key features include environment pinning, versioned data, workflow orchestration, and deterministic randomness.
Use cases span scientific computing, software engineering, and data science where auditability is critical.
It matters because it eliminates friction caused by process inconsistencies rather than technological limitations.
knowledge/concepts/reproducible-research.summary: Reproducible research requires four layers: environment pinning, versioned data, workflow orchestration, and deterministic randomness. Environment pinning prioritizes `uv` for Python, `pixi` for mixed dependencies, `renv` for R, and `Project.toml`/`Manifest.toml` for Julia, with containers used for system-level dependencies. Data must be versioned via content-addressable hashes using tools like DVC, Git LFS, or S3 manifests, ensuring every file has a recorded hash and provenance. Workflow orchestration replaces fragile shell scripts with DAG-based engines like Snakemake (Python-heavy) or Nextflow (bioinformatics), which handle parallelism and partial reruns. Deterministic randomness mandates explicit seeding at every entry point for libraries like NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn, while acknowledging GPU non-determinism limits. Notebooks require disciplined execution (top-to-bottom), stripping outputs from version control, and moving reusable logic to source files. Finally, provenance capture automatically logs commit hashes, environment digests, and execution metadata to ensure full traceability.

knowledge/concepts/reward-shaping-intrin.title: Reward Shaping & Intrinsic Reward Design in RL
knowledge/concepts/reward-shaping-intrin.description:
Reward shaping and intrinsic reward design are techniques that modify RL reward signals to accelerate learning without altering the optimal policy.
Key features include addressing sparse and delayed rewards, preventing reward hacking, and ensuring alignment with designer intent.
These methods are used in complex environments like robotics and games where feedback is infrequent or misaligned.
They matter because they solve critical challenges like long learning times and the difficulty of defining perfect reward functions.
knowledge/concepts/reward-shaping-intrin.summary: Reward Shaping and Intrinsic Reward Design are techniques in Reinforcement Learning (RL) that modify reward signals to accelerate learning and address sparse rewards, delayed feedback, and reward hacking without altering the optimal policy. Reward Engineering defines the initial function $R(s,a,s')$, while Reward Shaping adds a potential-based term $R'(s,a,s') = R(s,a,s') + \gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s)$ to provide incremental guidance; this guarantees policy invariance because the value function shifts only by a constant $\Phi(s)$. Common shaping strategies include using heuristics like Manhattan or Euclidean distance to encourage progress toward goals. Intrinsic Reward Design employs meta-learning (e.g., Policy Gradient for Reward Design) to dynamically optimize reward parameters and combines extrinsic rewards with intrinsic signals like progress, prediction error, or diversity to reduce sample complexity. Practical implementations must mitigate pitfalls such as reward sparsity, hacking, and misalignment using solutions like sub-goals, multi-objective vector rewards, and iterative validation. Modern approaches integrate adaptive shaping coefficients, language-guided shaping via LLMs, and learned reward functions from trajectories to handle complex, multi-objective tasks efficiently.

knowledge/concepts/rotary-positional-emb.title: Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)
knowledge/concepts/rotary-positional-emb.description:
Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) encodes token positions as rotations in 2D subspaces to enable models to understand relative distances without learnable parameters.
It unifies absolute and relative positional encoding while maintaining compatibility with efficient attention mechanisms like FlashAttention.
This technique serves as the standard positional encoding for major open-weight LLMs and supports context length extension methods for handling massive sequences.
RoPE matters because it offers a computationally efficient, parameter-free solution that naturally handles long-range dependencies and generalizes to structured data.
knowledge/concepts/rotary-positional-emb.summary: Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), introduced by Su et al. (2021), encodes token positions as rotations in 2D subspaces, ensuring attention depends solely on relative distance. It unifies absolute and relative encoding with zero learnable parameters and serves as the standard for major LLMs (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Qwen). The method applies rotation matrices based on dimension-specific frequencies to query and key vectors before attention computation. Key properties include true relative position encoding, natural recency bias, compatibility with efficient attention mechanisms (FlashAttention), and multi-dimensional generalization. While vanilla RoPE cannot extrapolate beyond training lengths, extension methods like Position Interpolation, NTK-aware Interpolation, YaRN (the current production standard), and LongRoPE enable context windows from 4K to over 2M tokens. Performance overhead is minimal (~1-3% compute). RoPE outperforms alternatives like ALiBi in downstream tasks but faces theoretical limits regarding angular resolution at extreme lengths, prompting emerging alternatives like ComRoPE and Resonance RoPE.

knowledge/concepts/saas-pricing-psycholo.title: SaaS Pricing Psychology for Solo Founders
knowledge/concepts/saas-pricing-psycholo.description:
This node provides actionable pricing strategies specifically tailored for solo SaaS founders managing products with self-serve checkouts and MRR under $50K.
It emphasizes using anchoring techniques to frame price perception and implementing a Good–Better–Best three-tier structure to guide buyers toward the most profitable middle option.
The content advises selecting value metrics like outcomes or usage that align with customer success rather than relying on arbitrary feature gates.
Adopting these principles allows founders to significantly boost operating profits by optimizing price sensitivity and avoiding the common mistake of leaving money on the table.
knowledge/concepts/saas-pricing-psycholo.summary:
Pricing is the highest-leverage lever for solo SaaS founders, where a 1% price increase yields ~10x the profit impact of a 1% volume increase. This guidance targets self-serve products ($0–50K MRR) with free tiers and individual buyers.

**Core Strategies:**
*   **Anchoring:** Use a high-anchor plan (left/top) to make others feel like savings; use crossed-out prices only for genuine discounts; avoid single-plan pages.
*   **Good-Better-Best Structure:** Adopt a 3-tier model where the middle tier is the intended target. Use price ratios of roughly 1:2.5:6 (e.g., $19/$49/$129). Avoid tight spreads (1:1.5:2) that cause decision paralysis.
*   **Value Metric:** Prioritize charging by **Outcome** or **Usage** for alignment. Use **Flat** or **Seats** for early stages; avoid usage-based billing until instrumentation is ready.
*   **Annual Discounts:** Offer 17% ("2 months free") as the standard to shift cash flow and reduce churn. Increase to 20% for confidence signals or 30%+ only if high churn requires immediate cash.
*   **Price Endings:** Use charm pricing ($X9) under $50/mo; switch to round numbers ($X0) for B2B tools over $99/mo to signal professionalism. Align prices with buyer expense-approval thresholds (e.g., $499 vs $549).

**Lifecycle & Execution:**
*   **Pre-launch:** Ship one plan immediately.
*   **<$1K MRR:** Learn value metrics via customer talks; do not optimize price yet.
*   **$1–10K MRR:** Introduce annual billing and a higher tier; grandfather existing customers.
*   **$10–50K MRR:** Add a third tier; test 20% price hikes on new signups.
*   **>$50K MRR:** Transition to usage/hybrid models and hire billing support.

**Critical Mistakes to Avoid:** Under-pricing to appear accessible (signals low quality), frequent price changes (confuses customers/SEO), omitting annual plans, displaying all features in every tier (hides upgrade value), and hiding prices behind "contact us" forms for self-serve products.

knowledge/concepts/saas-pricing-rollout-.title: SaaS Pricing Rollout Playbook
knowledge/concepts/saas-pricing-rollout-.description:
The SaaS Pricing Rollout Playbook treats pricing changes as software releases to prevent revenue leakage from botched deployments.
It defines three migration strategies: new signups only, grandfathering with a sunset window, and immediate migration for catastrophic errors.
The guide advises against A/B testing prices for solo founders due to insufficient traffic and operational complexity.
It matters because a flawed rollout can cause more revenue loss than the pricing miscalibration it attempts to fix.
knowledge/concepts/saas-pricing-rollout-.summary: A SaaS pricing rollout is a deployment requiring a defined audience, measurement plan, rollback criteria, and communication sequence. The primary decision is determining who pays the new price: Option 1 (new signups only) is the default low-risk choice for indie founders under $25K MRR; Option 2 (grandfather with a 6–12 month sunset window) applies when old pricing was under-priced and loss cannot be sustained; Option 3 (immediate migration) is reserved for catastrophic pricing errors and expects 10–30% churn. Solo founders should generally use a single cutover with an 8–12 week measurement window rather than A/B testing, which requires high traffic and complex tooling. Key metrics to track include conversion rate, ARPU, time-to-upgrade, churn-by-tier, and revenue mix. Decision triggers at week 8 dictate whether to accept, iterate, or rollback based on MRR projections and churn spikes. Communication strategies range from light touches for new-signup-only changes to heavy, pre-announced sequences for sunset windows, avoiding apologetic tones and burying the price change. Operational rules for grandfathering must define lock-in duration, handling of upgrades/downgrades/cancellations, and the loss of grandfather status upon resubscription.

knowledge/concepts/safe-install.md.title: Safe-Install — Content-Based Service Detection
knowledge/concepts/safe-install.md.description:
Safe-Install is a content-based service detection mechanism that probes backing services by fingerprinting HTTP responses instead of checking container names.
It classifies services into four states—running, vct-managed, foreign, or incompatible—to determine whether to start, adopt, or abort installation.
The system supports three conflict resolution strategies including using alternative ports, adopting foreign services, or aborting the process.
This approach allows the orchestrator to coexist safely with foreign services on canonical ports without modifying them or relying on container metadata.
knowledge/concepts/safe-install.md.summary:
**Safe-Install** enables content-based service detection in `install.py`, allowing the orchestrator to coexist with foreign services on canonical ports by fingerprinting HTTP responses instead of checking container names. It distinguishes between **Safe-Install** (service detection) and **Safe add** (project `.env` protection).

**Detection Logic**: Probes ports 8081 (Weaviate), 11435 (Ollama), and 11440 (code-embed) to classify services into four states:
*   **not running**: Start orchestrator container.
*   **vct-managed**: Auto-adopt based on `~/.vct/services.toml` entries.
*   **foreign**: Response matches but no `services.toml` entry; triggers interactive prompts.
*   **incompatible**: Content mismatch (e.g., Postgres on port 8081); refuses execution.

**Conflict Resolution (`--on-conflict`)**:
*   **alt-port (default)**: Generates `infrastructure/docker-compose.override.yml` to run on the next free port, preserving the existing service.
*   **adopt**: Writes vco collections into the foreign service (requires explicit opt-in and spare capacity).
*   **abort**: Terminates installation.

**Adoption Lock**: The `~/.vct/services.toml` file persists resolved actions (e.g., `mode: "adopt"`, `parallel_port`). `install.py` uses a hand-rolled TOML writer to ensure compatibility before `pip-install`.

**Collection Naming**: When adopting Weaviate, collection names are derived from the project basename (PascalCased) or explicit env vars to prevent namespace pollution. The system skips creation if collections exist, avoids bare `Development` collections if `<X>_development` is present, and prevents auto-adopting cross-project shared Knowledge Graphs.

**Flags**:
*   `--skip-seed`: Skips seeding and collection bootstrap.
*   `--skip-collections`: Skips creating new collections but seeds existing ones.

**Technical Update (2026-05-06)**: The probe endpoint for Weaviate readiness was changed from `/v1/.well-known/ready` (prone to false negatives/503 errors) to `/v1/meta` across all launcher detection sites to accurately reflect service usability.

knowledge/concepts/saga-pattern-distribu.title: Saga Pattern for Distributed Workflows
knowledge/concepts/saga-pattern-distribu.description:
The Saga Pattern enables distributed workflows by chaining local transactions with compensating actions to handle failures across multiple systems.
It ensures consistency without global transactions by reversing the effects of completed steps when a failure occurs in the sequence.
Two orchestration styles exist: choreography uses event-driven decoupling, while orchestration relies on a central coordinator for linear control.
This pattern matters because it allows complex multi-system processes like order fulfillment to remain resilient and consistent despite individual service failures.
knowledge/concepts/saga-pattern-distribu.summary: The Saga Pattern enables distributed workflows across multiple systems by executing a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a specific compensation operation to reverse its effects upon failure. Unlike database rollbacks, compensations are forward operations (e.g., refunds, cancellations) that maintain eventual consistency. Implementation styles include **Choreography** (event-driven, decoupled but harder to debug) and **Orchestration** (central coordinator, easier to reason about but requires durable execution engines to prevent state loss). Key design rules mandate that every step has a compensation, all compensations must be idempotent and commutative where possible, and state must be persisted durably (via engines, database rows, or event sourcing) rather than in memory. The pattern accepts eventual consistency and lower latency in exchange for the complexity of handling partial failures, contrasting with Two-Phase Commit (2PC) which offers strong consistency but suffers from poor liveness under network partitions.

knowledge/concepts/sales-funnel-stages-2.title: Sales Funnel Stages and Bow-Tie Model 2026
knowledge/concepts/sales-funnel-stages-2.description:
This framework extends the traditional sales funnel to include post-sale growth stages like onboarding and advocacy.
It balances acquisition efforts with retention metrics to ensure sustainable revenue compounding.
The model treats the contract signing as a central pinch point connecting pre-sales and post-sales operations.
It matters because high net revenue retention allows businesses to grow without constantly acquiring new logos.
knowledge/concepts/sales-funnel-stages-2.summary: The classic TOFU/MOFU/BOFU funnel, designed for early 2010s outbound B2B, serves as a useful content-planning framework but fails as an operational model because it ignores 60% of the customer lifecycle. The modern **Bow-Tie Model** extends the funnel through acquisition (left side) and retention (right side), treating them as equally weighted. While the left side focuses on lead-to-opportunity conversion, the right side drives Net Revenue Retention (NRR); businesses with NRR > 100% grow via compounding existing revenue, whereas those with NRR < 100% must constantly acquire new logos just to maintain status. Critical post-sales stages include Onboarding, Activation (the most vital metric, defined by specific product actions), Health, Expansion, Renewal, and Advocacy. Attribution should move beyond first/last-touch extremes toward multi-touch models (U-shaped, W-shaped, time-decay) or data-driven approaches, acknowledging that attributed pipeline often overstates incremental value. The funnel remains valid as a diagnostic tool for mapping content intent and identifying leakage points (e.g., low MQLs indicate reach issues, low SQLs indicate qualification problems), but it must be viewed as a stylized model rather than a literal representation of non-linear buyer behavior.

knowledge/concepts/scientific-paper-tria.title: Scientific Paper Triage Schema
knowledge/concepts/scientific-paper-tria.description:
The Scientific Paper Triage Schema is a structured framework that converts a collection of research papers into a comparable table for efficient ranking.
It extracts standardized metadata including citation details, study design, sample sizes, and methodological quality indicators like randomization and blinding.
Researchers use this schema to quickly filter large volumes of PDFs, identify methodological flaws, and prioritize which papers warrant deep reading.
This system matters because it saves weeks of reading time while surfacing statistical pitfalls that should temper trust in specific paper claims.
knowledge/concepts/scientific-paper-tria.summary: This schema streamlines the triage of 30+ scientific PDFs by converting them into a comparable table, enabling ranking by relevance and surfacing methodological flaws. It defines a field-agnostic extraction structure (citation, study type, sample sizes, randomization, blinding, effect sizes, etc.) with strict rules to report missing data explicitly rather than guessing. A fixed critical-appraisal checklist flags specific risks like pseudoreplication, missing effect sizes, lack of multiple-comparison correction, and HARKing, requiring one-sentence reasons for each flag. Post-extraction synthesis involves clustering themes, synthesizing effect sizes, identifying gaps, and resolving contradictions to generate a priority list of 5-10 papers. The output is structured into a TSV table, flagged claims file, synthesis narrative, and optional per-paper notes, while adhering to PRISMA 2020 and CAMARADES standards for systematic reviews. The schema acts as a filter for careful reading and flags methodological concerns but does not replace full paper review, assess scientific novelty, extract data from figures, or judge the ultimate validity of claims.

knowledge/concepts/score-driven-retrieva.title: Score-Driven Retrieval Tiers
knowledge/concepts/score-driven-retrieva.description:
Score-Driven Retrieval Tiers is a per-result verbosity policy that adjusts content detail based on relevance scores.
It replaces uniform detail parameters to save tokens on low-score results while enriching high-score hits.
The system applies five calibrated tiers ranging from discarding noise to returning full node content.
This approach optimizes context budgets for agents by preventing redundant re-calls for deeper detail.
knowledge/concepts/score-driven-retrieva.summary: Score-Driven Retrieval Tiers is a per-result verbosity policy implemented in the Weaviate MCP server that adjusts content richness based on search relevance scores, replacing the previous uniform `detail` parameter. This system normalizes scores to 0..1 and applies five calibrated tiers: `discard` (<0.42), `summary` (0.42–0.55), `single_chunk` (0.55–0.65), `three_chunks` (0.65–0.75), and `full` (≥0.75). It is applied by `hybrid_search`, `semantic_graph_search`, and the pre-edit hook (`rl_kg_search.py`), where connected nodes in graph searches default to `summary` to avoid latency. The policy relies on a sidecar file (`knowledge/.node_formats.json`) for LLM-generated descriptions and chunk summaries, with fallbacks to shorter summaries or content snippets if missing. Tunable thresholds are defined in `_TIER_THRESHOLDS` and environment variables. The implementation yields approximately 57% token savings compared to uniform `full` retrieval while ensuring the highest-relevance results retain full detail. Explicit `detail` overrides bypass score-based logic, and RL reranker failures silently fall back to distance-based ordering without surfacing a fallback flag.

knowledge/concepts/semantic-search.md.title: Semantic Search
knowledge/concepts/semantic-search.md.description:
Semantic search retrieves documents based on meaning by encoding queries and content as dense vectors in a shared embedding space.
It uses embedding models like qwen3-embedding or BGE-M3 to convert text into numerical representations for similarity comparison.
The technology enables finding conceptually related content even when query terms differ significantly from the document's vocabulary.
Hybrid search implementations combine dense vector retrieval with sparse keyword matching to capture both semantic and exact matches.
This approach is essential for building intelligent RAG systems that understand user intent beyond simple keyword matching.
Performance is optimized using Approximate Nearest Neighbor algorithms like HNSW to balance speed and recall in large datasets.
knowledge/concepts/semantic-search.md.summary:
**Semantic Search** retrieves documents based on meaning by encoding queries and documents as dense vectors in a shared embedding space, enabling the discovery of conceptually related content beyond exact keyword matches. The process involves an **Embedding Phase** (processing documents into vectors stored in a database) and a **Query Phase** (embedding the user query and performing nearest neighbor search using metrics like Cosine similarity or Dot product). While pure semantic search captures meaning, **Hybrid Search** combines dense vector retrieval with sparse keyword matching (BM25) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion to ensure exact matches are not missed.

**Implementation** typically utilizes **Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)** algorithms like HNSW for performance, with optimal chunking strategies (256–512 tokens with 20–50 token overlap) balancing precision and recall. This technique serves as the retrieval backbone for **RAG** systems. Key considerations include selecting appropriate embedding models (e.g., `qwen3-embedding:0.6b` for text, `CodeSage-Large-v2` for code), managing the trade-off between chunk size and retrieval quality, and following production best practices such as batch encoding, normalization, and monitoring for embedding drift. Fine-tuning is recommended when generic models fail to capture specific domain nuances.

knowledge/concepts/shared-knowledge-grap.title: Shared Knowledge Graph (Cross-Project)
knowledge/concepts/shared-knowledge-grap.description:
It is a cross-project knowledge graph in Weaviate that seeds reusable concepts like architecture notes and RAG patterns for all projects on a machine.
Key features include transparent merging of per-project and shared results, automatic de-duplication and re-ranking, and legacy collection name compatibility without data migration.
Use cases involve enabling junior projects to instantly access expert knowledge such as FlashAttention details without re-learning or re-seeding data.
It matters because it prevents redundant learning of common concepts while ensuring consistent, high-quality answers across the entire system through a single Weaviate instance.
knowledge/concepts/shared-knowledge-grap.summary:
The Vibecoded Orchestrator includes a single, machine-wide **Shared Knowledge Graph (Weaviate collection: `VibeCodedOrchestrator_KnowledgeGraph`)** seeded at install time with curated bundled nodes. Every project queries both its own per-project KG and this shared KG by default; results are merged, de-duplicated, and re-ranked together to ensure reusable knowledge (e.g., architecture notes, RAG patterns) is accessible across all projects without re-learning.

**Architecture & Data Flow:**
*   **Collections:** One shared collection exists alongside multiple per-project collections within a single Weaviate instance.
*   **MCP Server:** The `weaviate_mcp/server.py` transparently queries both collections, merges results by title/chunk, keeps the best score per key, and applies RL-rerank/auto-tiering.
*   **Seeding:** Curated nodes materialize once into the orchestrator root (`knowledge/`) via `install.py` and sync to Weaviate. Non-root projects read exclusively from the shared KG.
*   **Legacy Support:** Legacy collection names are recognized; users can designate a different collection as canonical via the launcher's Identity tab without data migration.

**Read/Write Behavior:**
*   **Read:** Unconditional and default for all projects. Results include a `collection` field for disambiguation.
*   **Write:** Default scope is `"project"`. Writing to the shared KG requires explicit `scope="shared"` to prevent noise pollution.
*   **Opt-Out:** `SHARED_KG_READ_DISABLED` excludes the shared KG from reads; `SHARED_KG_WRITE_DISABLED` blocks writes to the shared scope.

**Sidecars & Tiering:**
*   Sidecar resolution (`.node_formats.json`) is per-collection, routing based on the result's `collection` field.
*   The shared KG flows through the same 5-tier retrieval pipeline (`discard` to `full`) with uniform threshold env vars.

**Failure Modes & Constraints:**
*   **Missing Shared KG:** Queries return empty for the shared side but continue using the project KG; the installer recreates the collection on next run.
*   **Orphan Prune:** The installer does **not** auto-adopt foreign shared KGs (e.g., from previous installs) because the `orphan-prune` process deletes entries whose source files no longer exist, preventing silent data loss between installations.
*   **Foreign Sharing:** Power-users can override `SHARED_KG_COLLECTION` for cross-machine sharing but must manage orphan-prune collisions themselves.

knowledge/concepts/sli-selection-methodo.title: SLI Selection Methodology
knowledge/concepts/sli-selection-methodo.description:
SLI Selection Methodology is a judgment-based process for defining the correct Service Level Indicator to avoid alerting failures or missing user complaints.
It answers three critical questions about the user, the meaning of success, and the measurement source before writing any monitoring queries.
The methodology categorizes services by shape to recommend primary and secondary SLIs like availability, latency, or throughput.
It enforces a specific mathematical formulation where every SLI is expressed as a ratio of good events to valid events.
This approach ensures that monitoring accurately reflects user happiness and prevents SLOs from becoming decorative or misleading.
knowledge/concepts/sli-selection-methodo.summary: Choosing the correct Service Level Indicator (SLI) is the critical judgment call in SLO design, as incorrect choices lead to false positives/negatives or unrepresentative user happiness metrics. The selection process requires answering three questions: identifying the user (human vs. system), defining what "worked" means for that user, and determining the measurement vantage point (server-side vs. client-side vs. synthetic), often necessitating a layered approach. SLIs should be formulated as the ratio of *good events* to *valid events*, where valid events exclude non-user traffic (e.g., `/health` endpoints) and client errors (4xx) for availability, but include all requests for latency calculations. Latency thresholds must be derived from user research rather than current percentiles to avoid circular logic. Measurement should combine canonical server-side metrics for the SLO with Real User Monitoring (RUM) for diagnostics and synthetic probes for low-traffic backstops. Common pitfalls include using resource metrics (CPU/memory) as SLIs, applying a single SLI to a complex workflow, or failing to distinguish between service failures and dependency outages. A robust setup typically employs 2–3 SLIs per service (e.g., availability, latency, throughput) across stable alerting windows, adjusting for traffic patterns like bursts or low volume.

knowledge/concepts/slo-error-budget-mult.title: SLO Error Budgets and Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alerts
knowledge/concepts/slo-error-budget-mult.description:
This concept defines a reliability management strategy that uses error budgets and multi-window burn-rate alerts to prevent static threshold pitfalls.
It calculates how fast an error budget is being consumed across short and long time windows to balance rapid outage detection with stability.
Engineers use this approach to distinguish between transient spikes and sustained leaks that threaten to exhaust the entire monthly error budget.
It matters because it provides precise urgency signals that guide whether to page on-call engineers immediately or create a standard ticket.
knowledge/concepts/slo-error-budget-mult.summary:
**Service Level Objectives (SLOs)** define target reliability levels, with the **error budget** representing the permissible failure amount. **Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts** monitor budget consumption speed across short and long observation windows to ensure alerts are both rapid (catching outages quickly) and stable (avoiding flapping). Unlike static thresholds that either miss slow leaks or trigger on transient spikes, burn-rate alerting quantifies urgency by calculating how fast the budget is depleted relative to the SLO window.

The **burn rate** is the ratio of the current error rate to the error budget. A burn rate of `1` depletes the budget over the full SLO window, while higher rates indicate faster depletion. Effective alerting requires pairing a **short window** (for quick recovery detection) with a **long window** (to prevent flapping). Google SRE recommends specific tiers:
*   **Page (Urgent):** Burn rate ≥ 14.4 (exhausts budget in ~2 days).
*   **Page (Slower):** Burn rate ≥ 6 (exhausts budget in ~5 days).
*   **Ticket:** Burn rate ≥ 1 (exhausts budget in ~10 days).

Implementation typically uses recording rules to pre-compute error rates for multiple windows, with alerting rules requiring thresholds to be exceeded in both short and long windows simultaneously. This approach applies to both availability SLOs and latency SLOs (using histogram quantiles). Common pitfalls include using single-window thresholds, counting expected 5xx errors, measuring from the wrong vantage point (e.g., inside the app rather than at the edge), including non-product traffic in SLIs, and inconsistent window definitions.

knowledge/concepts/solo-saas-launch-play.title: Solo SaaS Launch Playbook
knowledge/concepts/solo-saas-launch-play.description:
The Solo SaaS Launch Playbook is a strategic guide for founders to coordinate multi-channel communications for single product releases.
